rules.title: The cramfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The cramfs module implements support for the Compressed ROM filesystem. It is obsolete and is not used on modern systems, and disabling it removes the ability to mount malicious cramfs images.
rules.impact: If the module is loaded, an attacker can mount a specially crafted cramfs image to exploit vulnerabilities in its parser and execute code with kernel privileges.

rules.title: The freevxfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The freevxfs module provides support for the Veritas filesystem. It is not used in standard Linux deployments, and disabling it reduces the kernel attack surface.
rules.impact: The availability of rarely used filesystem modules increases the kernel attack surface. A vulnerability in the freevxfs parser can be used for privilege escalation.

rules.title: The hfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The hfs module implements support for the Apple HFS filesystem. It is not required on Linux servers, and disabling it reduces the risk of exploiting vulnerabilities in the implementation.
rules.impact: A loaded hfs module can be used to mount a malicious image and exploit kernel parser vulnerabilities in order to execute arbitrary code.

rules.title: The hfsplus kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The hfsplus module supports the extended Apple HFS+ filesystem. It is not used on Linux servers, and disabling it removes the associated attack vector.
rules.impact: The presence of the hfsplus module allows a local attacker to mount a malicious image and exploit kernel vulnerabilities to gain elevated privileges.

rules.title: The jffs2 kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The jffs2 module supports a filesystem for flash memory. It is not needed on servers with traditional disks, and disabling it reduces the kernel code available for exploitation.
rules.impact: A vulnerability in the jffs2 handler can be used to corrupt kernel memory or execute code with kernel privileges when a malicious device is mounted.

rules.title: The overlay kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The kernel module overlay, known as Overlayfs, implements a union filesystem and allows one filesystem to be layered on top of another, creating a single view.
rules.impact: Known vulnerabilities in the overlay module are CVE-2023-32629, CVE-2023-2640, and CVE-2023-0386. If the module is available, an attacker can exploit them or execute setuid files without authorization and escalate privileges.

rules.title: The squashfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: Squashfs is a compressed read-only filesystem used mainly for LiveCD images. It is unnecessary on servers, and disabling it reduces the kernel code base.
rules.impact: Availability of the squashfs module allows arbitrary images to be mounted and vulnerabilities in the kernel parser to be exploited. It can also be used for covert storage of malicious data.

rules.title: The udf kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The udf filesystem implements the Universal Disk Format defined by ISO/IEC 13346 and ECMA-167 and is used to store data on optical media, including DVD.
rules.impact: If udf support is not required but the module remains available, the local attack surface increases. An attacker can mount a crafted udf image and exploit vulnerabilities in its kernel parser.

rules.title: The firewire-core kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The IEEE 1394 bus, known as FireWire, is a serial bus for high-speed real-time data transfer. It is not typically used on modern servers.
rules.impact: If the firewire-core module is loaded, an attacker with physical access can read and modify system memory through a FireWire port, and can exploit driver flaws to execute code in the kernel.

rules.title: The usb-storage kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The usb-storage module allows USB drives to be attached and is not needed on servers where users have no physical access. Disabling it prevents unauthorized connection of external media.
rules.impact: Without restrictions on USB drives, an attacker with physical access can steal data, load malware, or bypass security policies through external media.

rules.title: The unused filesystems kernel modules are not available
rules.explanation: Filesystem modules are loaded into the Linux kernel dynamically and extend its ability to work with filesystems. Unused modules should be disabled or prevented from loading.
rules.impact: Loadable modules let an attacker hide processes and files, a technique used by rootkits. Known vulnerabilities exist in the ceph, cifs, exfat, ext, fat, fscache, fuse, gfs2, nfs_common, nfsd, and smbfs_common modules.

rules.title: /tmp is tmpfs or a separate partition
rules.explanation: Placing /tmp on a separate partition limits DoS attacks that fill the disk and allows specific mount options to be applied. This is a basic server hardening practice.
rules.impact: Without a separate partition, a malicious process or user can fill all disk space through /tmp and cause a denial of service for the entire system.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on /tmp partition
rules.explanation: The nodev option prevents creation and use of block and character devices in /tmp. It is a standard protection for partitions that hold temporary files.
rules.impact: Without nodev, an attacker can create a device file in /tmp and use it to access hardware resources or bypass security policies.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on /tmp partition
rules.explanation: The nosuid option prevents execution of setuid/setgid programs from /tmp. It blocks privilege-escalation attempts that use specially crafted files.
rules.impact: Without nosuid, an attacker can place a setuid program in /tmp that runs with root privileges and fully compromises the system.

rules.title: The noexec option is set on /tmp partition
rules.explanation: The noexec option prevents binaries from being executed directly from /tmp. It is a critical protection that blocks most attack scenarios that use temporary storage.
rules.impact: Without noexec, an attacker who has uploaded a malicious file to /tmp can execute it immediately. This is one of the most common post-exploitation vectors on compromised systems.

rules.title: /dev/shm is tmpfs or a separate partition
rules.explanation: /dev/shm is a tmpfs partition for process shared memory, and mounting it separately allows restrictive options to be applied. This is standard for hardened systems.
rules.impact: Without isolating /dev/shm, a malicious process can use shared memory for inter-process communication, to bypass SELinux/AppArmor restrictions, and to attack other processes.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on /dev/shm partition
rules.explanation: The nodev option on /dev/shm prevents device files from being created in shared memory. It limits how this partition can be abused.
rules.impact: Device files in /dev/shm can be used by malicious processes to bypass device-access policies and gain unauthorized access to hardware resources.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on /dev/shm partition
rules.explanation: The nosuid option prevents execution of SUID/SGID programs from /dev/shm. It stops shared memory from being used for privilege-escalation attacks.
rules.impact: Without nosuid, an attacker can place a SUID file in /dev/shm to escalate privileges. This is especially dangerous in multi-user environments and where vulnerable applications are present.

rules.title: The noexec option is set on /dev/shm partition
rules.explanation: The noexec option prevents code from being executed from /dev/shm. This is a critical protection, because attackers often use /dev/shm to load and run payloads in memory.
rules.impact: Without noexec, /dev/shm becomes a convenient foothold for fileless attacks: malicious code is loaded into memory through /dev/shm and executed without leaving traces on disk.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /home
rules.explanation: A separate partition for /home isolates user data from system files. It prevents DoS through disk exhaustion by users and makes quota policies easier to apply.
rules.impact: Without isolation, a user process or an attacker can fill the root partition through /home, making the entire system inoperable and risking data loss.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on /home partition
rules.explanation: The nodev option on /home prevents device files from being created in users' home directories. Users should not be able to create such files.
rules.impact: Without nodev, a privileged user can create a device file in their home directory and use it for unauthorized access to system hardware resources.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on /home partition
rules.explanation: The nosuid option prevents SUID/SGID execution of files from home directories. It blocks a common privilege-escalation vector that uses prepared files in /home.
rules.impact: Without nosuid, an attacker with write access to /home can place a SUID file and use it to obtain another user's privileges or root.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var
rules.explanation: The /var partition holds variable data: logs, cache, and application temporary files. Isolation prevents the system partition from filling and keeps the system stable.
rules.impact: Filling /var through logs or application cache, without isolation, blocks writes to the root filesystem, disrupts system services, and creates conditions for a DoS attack.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on /var partition
rules.explanation: The nodev option on /var prevents device files from being created in the variable-data directory. Services that use /var should not create such files.
rules.impact: Device files in /var can be used by compromised services for direct access to hardware resources, bypassing the operating system's standard access-control mechanisms.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on /var partition
rules.explanation: The nosuid option prevents SUID programs from being started from /var. Legitimate applications should not place SUID files in /var, so this option is safe and recommended.
rules.impact: Without nosuid, malicious code that gains write access to /var, for example through a web-application vulnerability, can create a SUID file to escalate privileges.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/tmp
rules.explanation: /var/tmp is persistent temporary storage that survives reboots. Isolating it on a separate partition allows protective mount options to be applied.
rules.impact: Without isolating /var/tmp, an attacker can use this storage for long-term placement of malicious files and to fill the system partition for a DoS.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on /var/tmp partition
rules.explanation: The nodev option on /var/tmp forbids creation of device files in persistent temporary storage. It limits how this partition can be abused.
rules.impact: Without nodev, an attacker can create a device file in /var/tmp to bypass access control for hardware resources, using the fact that this partition persists across reboots.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on /var/tmp partition
rules.explanation: The nosuid option prevents execution of SUID programs from /var/tmp. This is especially important because the contents of this partition survive reboots.
rules.impact: Without nosuid, an attacker can place a SUID file in /var/tmp that remains after a reboot and provides a persistent privilege-escalation vector.

rules.title: The noexec option is set on /var/tmp partition
rules.explanation: The noexec option on /var/tmp blocks code execution from persistent temporary storage. This is a critical protection, because data in /var/tmp survives system reboots.
rules.impact: Without noexec, /var/tmp is an ideal place for persistent malicious code that survives a reboot. Attackers actively use this partition for long-term persistence.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/log
rules.explanation: A separate partition for /var/log protects logs from filling the system disk and preserves them. It also makes log access rights easier to configure.
rules.impact: Without isolating /var/log, filling the logs, whether intentional or accidental, blocks the root filesystem. An attacker can also fill the logs to destroy evidence.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on /var/log partition
rules.explanation: The nodev option on /var/log forbids device files in the log directory. It is a standard privilege restriction for partitions intended only to store data.
rules.impact: Without nodev, a compromised logging process can create a device file in /var/log to bypass hardware access-control mechanisms.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on /var/log partition
rules.explanation: The nosuid option on /var/log prevents execution of SUID files from the log directory. /var/log should not contain executables with elevated privileges.
rules.impact: Compromise of the logging subsystem, with write access to /var/log, would allow an attacker to place a SUID file if nosuid were not set.

rules.title: The noexec option is set on /var/log partition
rules.explanation: The noexec option prevents execution of files from /var/log. The log directory should not contain executable code, and this option enforces that in the kernel.
rules.impact: Without noexec, an attacker who can write to /var/log can plant an executable and run it. This is especially relevant when logging daemons are compromised.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/log/audit
rules.explanation: A separate partition for audit logs preserves them when other logs fill up. This is critical for regulatory requirements and for incident investigation.
rules.impact: Without isolating /var/log/audit, an attacker can fill the logs with ordinary data and destroy audit records. That violates compliance requirements and hides traces of the attack.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on /var/log/audit partition
rules.explanation: The nodev option on the audit partition prevents creation of device files in the store of critical logs. The audit directory should contain only log files.
rules.impact: A device file created in /var/log/audit can be used by a compromised service to gain direct access to hardware resources, bypassing standard access control.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on /var/log/audit partition
rules.explanation: The nosuid option on the audit partition forbids SUID execution of files in the log store. The audit directory should be protected against use as a foothold for attacks.
rules.impact: A SUID file in /var/log/audit that a compromised audit process could write would become a privilege-escalation vector when executed by another user.

rules.title: The noexec option is set on /var/log/audit partition
rules.explanation: The noexec option ensures that files in /var/log/audit cannot be executed directly. The audit partition is intended solely for storing logs.
rules.impact: Without noexec, compromise of auditd would let an attacker write a malicious executable into /var/log/audit and execute it, exploiting trust in the audit directory.

rules.title: The source.list and .source files use the Signed-By option
rules.explanation: APT source lists in /etc/apt/sources.list and /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ support an arbitrary number of repositories. The Signed-By option requires a repository to be verified by a specific set of keys, rather than by every key trusted by APT.
rules.impact: Without binding a repository to specific keys, any trusted key on the system can sign its metadata. That increases the risk of substituting the source and installing malicious software.

rules.title: The weak dependencies are configured
rules.explanation: The Debian package specification allows three dependency levels: hard (Requires), weak (Recommends), and suggestions (Suggests). The setting determines whether weak dependencies are installed automatically.
rules.impact: If weak dependencies are installed by default, the system gains packages it does not need. Each extra package and its services expands the attack surface and may contain vulnerabilities.

rules.title: The access to gpg key files are configured
rules.explanation: GPG key files are the cryptographic keys with which APT verifies the authenticity and integrity of packages. They are stored in /etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d or /usr/share/keyrings and are named in repository configuration through the signed-by option.
rules.impact: Key files are APT trust anchors. If an unprivileged user can write them, that user can replace or add a key for a fraudulent repository, and APT will install compromised packages as legitimate.

rules.title: The access to /etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d directory is configured
rules.explanation: The directory /etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d contains separate GPG key files that APT uses to verify the authenticity of packages and repositories. Access to the directory should be limited to the superuser.
rules.impact: If an unprivileged user can write to the directory, that user can replace APT trust keys and cause the system to accept packages from a controlled or fraudulent repository.

rules.title: The access to /etc/apt/auth.conf.d directory is configured
rules.explanation: The directory /etc/apt/auth.conf.d contains .conf files with credentials for access to private APT repositories. Access to the directory should be limited to the superuser.
rules.impact: The directory controls operation of the package manager as root and may contain confidential information. Read or write access for other users allows the configuration to be changed or credentials to be disclosed.

rules.title: The access to files in the /etc/apt/auth.conf.d/ directory is configured
rules.explanation: Files in the directory /etc/apt/auth.conf.d contain connection parameters and credentials for private APT repositories or proxies. Access to them should be limited to the superuser.
rules.impact: If the files are available to other users, logins and passwords for a proxy or repository can leak. With those credentials, an attacker can impersonate a trusted host and substitute the repository contents.

rules.title: The access to /usr/share/keyrings directory is configured
rules.explanation: The directory /usr/share/keyrings contains trusted GPG keyring files with which APT verifies signatures of packages from repositories. It is a centralized, read-only store of system keys.
rules.impact: If an unprivileged user can add or remove keys in this directory, that user can register their own key and open a path for the system to a repository of malicious packages.

rules.title: The access to /etc/apt/sources.list.d directory is configured
rules.explanation: The directory /etc/apt/sources.list.d allows sources.list entries to be placed in separate files. Access to the directory should be limited to the superuser.
rules.impact: The directory contains descriptions of the repositories used by APT. If an unprivileged user can add or remove files, that user can connect a repository of malicious packages.

rules.title: The access to files in /etc/apt/sources.list.d are configured
rules.explanation: Files in the directory /etc/apt/sources.list.d contain package-source entries as separate files. Access to them should be limited to the superuser.
rules.impact: The files define the repositories from which APT obtains packages. With insufficient permissions, an unprivileged user can change a source or add their own, which leads to installation of malicious software.

rules.title: The repositories are set to https in /etc/apt/sources.list
rules.explanation: APT supports access to repositories over HTTP and HTTPS. Official repositories use HTTPS by default, but third-party sources added by an administrator can be configured for unencrypted HTTP.
rules.impact: Over cleartext HTTP, an attacker between the system and the mirror can intercept metadata and block individual security updates. The system then remains with known vulnerabilities.

rules.title: The repositories are set to https in /etc/apt/sources.list.d directory
rules.explanation: APT supports access to repositories over HTTP and HTTPS. Official repositories use HTTPS by default, but third-party sources added by an administrator can be configured for unencrypted HTTP.
rules.impact: Over cleartext HTTP, an attacker between the system and the mirror can intercept metadata and block individual security updates. The system then remains with known vulnerabilities.

rules.title: AllowInsecureRepositories is configured
rules.explanation: The Acquire::AllowInsecureRepositories parameter determines whether APT is allowed to use repositories without a valid cryptographic signature on the InRelease or Release.gpg files. A value of 1 disables authenticity verification.
rules.impact: Allowing insecure repositories removes APT signature verification. An attacker capable of a man-in-the-middle attack, mirror compromise, or DNS substitution can deliver unsigned packages that the system installs as legitimate.

rules.title: AllowWeakRepositories is configured
rules.explanation: The Acquire::AllowWeakRepositories parameter determines whether APT accepts repositories signed with weak algorithms based on MD5 or SHA-1. A value of 0 requires strong signature algorithms.
rules.impact: MD5 and SHA-1 are cryptographically broken, and practical collision attacks exist against them. An attacker can produce malicious repository metadata that still passes signature verification.

rules.title: AllowDowngradeToInsecureRepositories is configured
rules.explanation: The Acquire::AllowDowngradeToInsecureRepositories parameter determines whether APT can silently switch to an insecure repository when the protected form of the same repository is unavailable. A value of 0 forbids that downgrade.
rules.impact: Allowing a silent downgrade creates a downgrade attack: an attacker blocks access to the protected repository and forces APT to use a controlled source of malicious packages.

rules.title: Acquire::Check-Date is configured
rules.explanation: The Acquire::Check-Date parameter determines whether APT checks that the system clock is plausible relative to the Valid-Until field in the repository Release file. When enabled, Release files with unacceptable dates are rejected.
rules.impact: Without the date check, an attacker on the communication path can replace the Release file with an older one, so APT treats the system as updated while it remains on vulnerable package versions. Known vulnerabilities then stay unpatched.

rules.title: The updates, patches, and additional security software are installed
rules.explanation: Updates and fixes for installed software are released periodically, either to remediate vulnerabilities or to extend functionality.
rules.impact: Until security fixes are installed, the system remains vulnerable to attacks that are already known and publicly described. An attacker can use ready-made exploits to take control of the host.

rules.title: The apparmor packages are installed
rules.explanation: AppArmor is a Mandatory Access Control (MAC) system that limits what programs can do at the kernel level, and it is a required security component of Ubuntu. Without it, confinement profiles are not applied.
rules.impact: Without AppArmor, a compromised application gets full access to system resources, limited only by the user's permissions. That greatly increases the damage from a compromise.

rules.title: AppArmor is enabled
rules.explanation: AppArmor is a kernel mechanism that confines programs to a defined set of resources by means of profiles. It is enabled by default on the target distributions.
rules.impact: Disabling AppArmor removes an additional layer of application isolation. If a service is compromised, an attacker can leave its profile, gain access to files and resources, and expand the attack.

rules.title: All AppArmor Profiles are enforcing
rules.explanation: enforce mode provides AppArmor's strongest protection: policy violations are blocked, not only logged. It is the recommended mode for production systems.
rules.impact: In complain mode, violations are only logged and are not blocked. A compromised application continues to run in violation of policy, so the attack can develop without obstruction.

rules.title: The kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_unconfined is enabled
rules.explanation: The kernel parameter kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_unconfined prevents an unprivileged process with an unconfined profile from using aa-exec to transition to a profile that is more advantageous to it.
rules.impact: Unconfined profiles can bypass the restriction on unprivileged user namespaces. After entering such a profile, a user can execute arbitrary code, or obtain a shell and escalate privileges.

rules.title: The bootloader password is set
rules.explanation: A GRUB bootloader password prevents unauthorized changes to boot parameters. Without it, an attacker with physical access can boot into single-user mode with no password.
rules.impact: Without a bootloader password, an attacker with physical access can add the init=/bin/bash parameter and obtain a root shell, completely bypassing operating-system authentication.

rules.title: The access to bootloader config is configured
rules.explanation: The GRUB configuration file contains password hashes and boot parameters. Mode 600 (root only) prevents unprivileged users from reading the hashes.
rules.impact: If grub.cfg is readable by ordinary users, they can obtain the bootloader password hash for an offline attack. Write access allows direct modification of the boot configuration.

rules.title: The fs.protected_hardlinks is configured
rules.explanation: The kernel parameter fs.protected_hardlinks controls creation of hard links to files. It restricts links to files that the user does not own and to which the user has no write permission.
rules.impact: When the protection is disabled, an attacker can create hard links to files the attacker cannot access. That opens exploitation of unsafe open or creat handling in privileged programs.

rules.title: The fs.protected_symlinks is configured
rules.explanation: The kernel parameter fs.protected_symlinks controls handling of symbolic links in world-writable directories, such as /tmp. It forbids following links that the user does not own.
rules.impact: Without this protection, an attacker plants symbolic links in publicly writable directories and, through unsafe open or creat handling in privileged programs, gains access to other users' files.

rules.title: The kernel.yama.ptrace_scope is configured
rules.explanation: The ptrace system call allows one process to observe the execution of another and to change its memory and registers. The kernel.yama.ptrace_scope parameter sets the tracing mode: 0 for classic permissions, 1 for a restriction, 2 for CAP_SYS_PTRACE only, and 3 for a complete prohibition.
rules.impact: If tracing is not restricted, a compromised application lets an attacker attach to other processes, such as Bash, Firefox, SSH sessions, or the GPG agent, and extract credentials and keys from them.

rules.title: The fs.suid_dumpable is configured
rules.explanation: The fs.suid_dumpable parameter determines whether a privileged setuid process can create a memory dump. The values are: 0, no dump is created; 1, allowed for all processes; 2, only when the dump is written to a full path.
rules.impact: Memory dumps can contain confidential data, including password hashes and keys. If privileged processes create dumps, an attacker can read them and obtain information for developing the attack.

rules.title: The kernel.dmesg_restrict is configured
rules.explanation: The kernel parameter kernel.dmesg_restrict denies unprivileged users access to information from the kernel log buffer. Viewing kernel messages remains available only to the superuser.
rules.impact: Without a restriction on access to the message buffer, an unprivileged user can obtain information about hardware, drivers, and kernel addresses. That makes it easier to select exploits and prepare an attack on the system.

rules.title: The prelink is not installed
rules.explanation: prelink is a program that modifies ELF shared libraries and dynamically linked executables so that they take less time to load. It is not required on modern systems.
rules.impact: prelink modifies binary files and interferes with integrity-checking tools such as AIDE. In addition, if a shared library such as libc is compromised, the vulnerability affects every prelinked program.

rules.title: Automatic Error Reporting is configured
rules.explanation: Apport is the system that automatically sends error reports to Canonical. It is undesirable on servers because it can disclose confidential information and generate unwanted outbound traffic.
rules.impact: Automatic error reports can contain memory fragments with confidential data. Apport also expands the attack surface and can be used to exploit vulnerabilities in the service itself.

rules.title: The kernel.kptr_restrict is configured
rules.explanation: The kernel.kptr_restrict parameter limits disclosure of kernel addresses through /proc and other interfaces. A value of 0 hashes the address, a value of 1 replaces %pK pointers with zeros, and a value of 2 does so regardless of privileges.
rules.impact: If kernel addresses are visible, an attacker can use /proc/kallsyms to determine the exact location of symbols and structures. That makes it easier to bypass kernel protections and to develop exploits for a specific build.

rules.title: The kernel.randomize_va_space is configured
rules.explanation: ASLR randomizes the placement of a process memory regions (stack, heap, and libraries), and a value of 2 enables full randomization. That makes most memory attacks substantially harder.
rules.impact: Without ASLR, an attacker can predict the addresses of functions and data in memory, which makes vulnerabilities such as buffer overflow, return-oriented programming (ROP), and use-after-free much easier to exploit.

rules.title: The core file size is configured
rules.explanation: The core setting in limits.conf limits the size of a memory-dump file, and the hard keyword sets a hard resource limit that the superuser establishes and that a user cannot exceed.
rules.impact: If the hard limit is not set, a user can raise the soft limit and obtain a memory dump of a process that crashed. Dumps contain confidential data, including passwords and keys.

rules.title: The systemd-coredump ProcessSizeMax is configured
rules.explanation: A core dump is a memory image of an executable program, used to determine why it crashed. The ProcessSizeMax parameter of the systemd-coredump service limits the maximum size of a dump that is processed.
rules.impact: Memory dumps contain a snapshot of process data, including confidential information. If the dump size is not limited, that data is stored on disk and becomes available to an attacker.

rules.title: The systemd-coredump Storage is configured
rules.explanation: A core dump is a memory image of an executable program, used to determine why it crashed. The Storage parameter of the systemd-coredump service determines whether dumps are saved and in which store.
rules.impact: If dumps are saved, memory snapshots that contain passwords, keys, and other confidential data remain on disk. An attacker with access to the system can read them and use them for further attacks.

rules.title: /etc/motd is configured
rules.explanation: The file /etc/motd contains the message of the day, which is shown to the user after a successful login. It is customary to place there a warning about the legal status of the system and the monitoring policy, without disclosing the OS version or the update level.
rules.impact: If the banner states the OS release and the patch level, an attacker gains information for selecting exploits for that specific system version. Without a warning about legal status and monitoring, holding an offender accountable is harder.

rules.title: /etc/issue is configured
rules.explanation: The file /etc/issue is read by agetty and similar programs and is displayed above the login prompt. Dynamic content is produced by issue-generator from files in /etc/issue.d, /run/issue.d, and /usr/lib/issue.d, and files from /etc/issue.d override same-named files from lower-priority directories.
rules.impact: If the login banner contains the OS name and version, an attacker uses that information to prepare an attack for that specific configuration. Without a warning about the legal status of the system and about monitoring, the organization's legal protection is reduced.

rules.title: /etc/issue.net is configured
rules.explanation: The file /etc/issue.net sets the banner shown to remote users before login through configured services. Its contents are static and do not depend on the terminal, and it is where a warning about the legal status of the system and the monitoring policy is placed.
rules.impact: If the remote-login banner states the OS version and the patch level, an attacker gains information for selecting exploits for that specific system. Without a warning about monitoring and the prohibition on unauthorized access, legal protection is harder.

rules.title: The pam_motd is configured
rules.explanation: The pam_motd module displays message-of-the-day files after a successful user login. By default it uses /etc/motd, /run/motd, /usr/lib/motd, and the matching .d directories: files from /etc override same-named files from /run and /usr/lib, and output follows lexicographic order of the names.
rules.impact: If pam_motd displays files from /run or /usr/lib that the administrator does not control, the user receives the OS version and the update level. That information helps an attacker select an exploit for the specific system.

rules.title: The sshd warning Banner is configured
rules.explanation: The Banner parameter in the sshd configuration specifies the file whose contents are sent to the remote user before authentication. This allows people who connect to be informed of the access rules and of a warning about the legal status of the system.
rules.impact: Without a configured sshd banner, users are not notified of the access policy and of monitoring, which creates legal and compliance risk. The default value does not state that unauthorized access is prohibited and reduces security awareness.

rules.title: The access to /etc/motd is configured
rules.explanation: The file /etc/motd should be owned by root and have mode 644 or stricter. This prevents unauthorized changes to the message for social engineering of users.
rules.impact: If /etc/motd is writable by unprivileged users, an attacker can replace its contents for phishing or to mislead users.

rules.title: The access to /etc/issue is configured
rules.explanation: The file /etc/issue should be owned by root. Correct permissions prevent attackers from substituting the login banner for social-engineering attacks.
rules.impact: Unauthorized modification of /etc/issue lets an attacker display fake warnings or request credentials from users before they log in.

rules.title: The access to /etc/issue.net is configured
rules.explanation: The file /etc/issue.net is displayed to remote users. Correct permissions of 644:root:root prevent unauthorized changes to it.
rules.impact: Changing /etc/issue.net lets an attacker show fake messages to every user attempting to connect over SSH, which creates a phishing vector.

rules.title: The access to pam_motd file is configured
rules.explanation: Files displayed by the pam_motd module (/etc/motd, /run/motd, /usr/lib/motd, and the .d directories) should be readable, but not writable by others. Ownership root:root and mode 644 or stricter prevent unprivileged users from replacing them.
rules.impact: With incorrect permissions, an unprivileged user can change pam_motd files and replace the warning with false or misleading information. That undermines trust in the banner and violates compliance requirements.

rules.title: The access to sshd warning banner is configured
rules.explanation: The sshd warning-banner file should be owned by the root user and the root group and should not be writable by the group or by other users. This ensures that only the system administrator changes the banner contents.
rules.impact: If the banner is writable by others, an attacker can remove the required warning text or insert misleading content. That weakens legal protection and misleads users about the rules for using the system.

rules.title: The update-notifier-motd.service is not in use
rules.explanation: update-notifier-motd.service is a systemd oneshot unit from the update-notifier-common package that updates dynamic MOTD fragments in /var/lib/update-notifier and, through /etc/update-motd.d/50-motd-news, contacts motd.ubuntu.com. The service should be stopped and masked; it is absent in Debian 13.
rules.impact: A dynamic MOTD discloses the number of packages and security updates, and the OS release, to anyone who sees the banner, including unauthenticated SSH connections. It also creates an unwanted dependency on the external host motd.ubuntu.com.

rules.title: The update-notifier-motd.timer is not in use
rules.explanation: update-notifier-motd.timer is a systemd timer from the update-notifier-common package that periodically starts update-notifier-motd.service to update dynamic MOTD fragments and integrate with motd-news. The timer should be stopped and masked; it is absent in Debian 13.
rules.impact: An unmasked timer keeps scheduling runs, creates noise in the log, and leaves a way to bring the service back quickly. An attacker or an operator with write access to the unit directories can unmask it and resume disclosure of information about the system.

rules.title: GDM login banner is configured
rules.explanation: If GDM is in use, the login screen should display a legal warning about authorized access. This is required for the security policy to have legal effect.
rules.impact: The absence of a warning at login can weaken the organization's legal position in security incidents and give an attacker the argument that access was not prohibited.

rules.title: GDM disable-user-list is configured
rules.explanation: GNOME Display Manager (GDM) provides graphical login on GNOME-based systems. The disable-user-list parameter prohibits display of the user list on the login screen, and lockdown mode in dconf prevents users from changing that setting.
rules.impact: Displaying the user list reveals half of the login-password pair and makes it easier to guess credentials for logging in. If system settings are not locked by lockdown mode, user dconf settings override them and the protection is turned off.

rules.title: GDM screen lock is configured
rules.explanation: GDM can lock the screen automatically when a user is idle. The idle-delay parameter sets the seconds of inactivity before the screen blanks, and lock-delay sets the delay before locking after blanking. Lockdown mode in dconf prevents users from changing these values.
rules.impact: Without automatic locking, another person can access a user session left unattended. If system settings are not protected by lockdown mode, a user can remove the lock and nullify the protection.

rules.title: GDM automount is configured
rules.explanation: By default, GNOME automatically mounts removable media when it is connected. The automount parameter in dconf disables that capability, and lockdown mode prevents users from changing the system setting in their sessions.
rules.impact: With automount enabled, a person with physical access can connect a USB drive or disk and obtain its contents even without permission to mount. That opens a path to infecting the system and to stealing data.

rules.title: GDM autorun-never is configured
rules.explanation: The autorun-never parameter prohibits GDM from automatically launching the contents of removable media. Lockdown mode in dconf prevents users from changing this setting and enforces it for every session.
rules.impact: Malware on removable media can use autorun when the media is connected and execute on the system. Without lockdown mode, user dconf settings take priority and can disable the autorun prohibition.

rules.title: XDMCP is not enabled
rules.explanation: XDMCP (X Display Manager Control Protocol) allows remote access to a graphical desktop over an unprotected protocol. On servers it should always be disabled.
rules.impact: XDMCP transmits data in the clear and does not support modern authentication. Enabled XDMCP allows remote takeover of a graphical session and is a serious vulnerability.

rules.title: Xwayland is configured
rules.explanation: Xwayland is a compatibility layer that lets legacy X11 applications run under Wayland: it is an X server running as a Wayland client. Disabling Xwayland removes the risks associated with the X11 legacy when X11 applications are not required.
rules.impact: Every X11 vulnerability, including keystroke capture, also applies to Xwayland, so malware can spy on input and intercept events of other X applications. Disabling Xwayland removes that attack surface.

rules.title: The autofs services are not in use
rules.explanation: autofs mounts filesystems automatically on demand. On servers it creates a risk of unauthorized mounting of network resources and local devices.
rules.impact: When autofs is active, arbitrary network resources can be mounted, which can be used for MITM attacks, theft of Kerberos credentials, and bypass of file access controls.

rules.title: The avahi daemon services are not in use
rules.explanation: Avahi implements mDNS/DNS-SD for automatic discovery of services on the local network (Zeroconf). On servers this is an unnecessary feature that expands the attack surface.
rules.impact: Avahi broadcasts information about available services on the network, which helps an attacker during reconnaissance. Vulnerabilities in Avahi can also be used for remote code execution.

rules.title: The dhcp server services are not in use
rules.explanation: A DHCP server assigns IP addresses to network clients. An unauthorized DHCP server can redirect client traffic through a gateway under an attacker's control.
rules.impact: An unauthorized DHCP server (rogue DHCP) can give clients malicious DNS servers and default gateways, which leads to traffic interception and DNS spoofing.

rules.title: The dns server services are not in use
rules.explanation: A DNS server (BIND9) should not run on hosts that are not intended for name resolution. A misconfigured DNS service can be used for attacks against the infrastructure.
rules.impact: An unauthorized DNS server can be used for DNS spoofing, cache poisoning, and to give an attacker a control channel through DNS tunneling.

rules.title: The dnsmasq services are not in use
rules.explanation: dnsmasq is a lightweight DHCP and DNS server. If it is not required for the system to operate, it should be disabled so it does not add to the attack surface.
rules.impact: An unnecessarily running dnsmasq provides unauthorized DHCP and DNS services, which can disrupt network configuration and enable man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks.

rules.title: The ftp server services are not in use
rules.explanation: FTP transmits data and credentials in cleartext without encryption. The protocol is obsolete and should be replaced by SFTP or SCP; on servers, the FTP server should be removed.
rules.impact: FTP transmits passwords in cleartext, so a sniffer can capture them. FTP servers have historically had many vulnerabilities, including directory traversal and arbitrary code execution.

rules.title: The ldap server services are not in use
rules.explanation: The LDAP server (slapd) provides directory services. If the host is not a domain controller or an LDAP server, slapd should be removed.
rules.impact: An unauthorized LDAP server can be used to intercept authentication on the network. Vulnerabilities in slapd can lead to unauthorized access to a directory that holds credentials.

rules.title: The message access server services are not in use
rules.explanation: IMAP/POP3 servers (Dovecot) are intended only for mail servers. On other systems, their presence creates an unnecessary attack surface.
rules.impact: An unnecessary IMAP/POP3 server expands the attack surface. Vulnerabilities in Dovecot can allow unauthorized access to mail data or arbitrary code execution.

rules.title: The network file system services are not in use
rules.explanation: NFS allows network filesystems to be mounted. On servers that do not explicitly need it, the NFS server should be disabled because of its complex security model.
rules.impact: NFS has historically had a weak security model. A misconfigured NFS service can grant unauthorized access to the filesystem or allow exports to be mounted without authentication.

rules.title: The nis server services are not in use
rules.explanation: NIS (Network Information Service) is an obsolete service that distributes credentials without encryption. It should not be used in modern infrastructure.
rules.impact: NIS transmits account data, including password hashes, without encryption. An attacker on the same network can capture all credentials and gain access to systems.

rules.title: The print server services are not in use
rules.explanation: CUPS is the printing service. On servers without printers it is unnecessary and adds to the attack surface; there are known cases of CUPS vulnerabilities being used for remote code execution (RCE).
rules.impact: Vulnerabilities in CUPS (including CVE-2024-47076 and related issues) allow remote code execution without authentication. Unnecessary CUPS creates a critical attack vector.

rules.title: The rpcbind services are not in use
rules.explanation: rpcbind is the port mapper for RPC services (NFS, NIS) and is required only when RPC services are in use. Disabling it removes a vector for scanning and for attacks against RPC.
rules.impact: rpcbind discloses information about active RPC services and is a historically vulnerable component. Its presence lets an attacker conduct reconnaissance of the RPC infrastructure.

rules.title: The rsync services are not in use
rules.explanation: The rsync daemon provides file synchronization over the network. In daemon mode without proper configuration, it can grant unauthorized access to the filesystem.
rules.impact: A misconfigured rsync daemon can open anonymous access to the server filesystem. Vulnerabilities in rsync have allowed arbitrary code execution on the server.

rules.title: The samba file server services are not in use
rules.explanation: Samba implements the SMB protocol for file sharing. If a file server for Windows clients is not required, Samba should be removed.
rules.impact: Samba is subject to serious vulnerabilities (including EternalBlue-like flaws). An unnecessary SMB service presents a broad attack surface and can be used for lateral movement on the network.

rules.title: The snmp services are not in use
rules.explanation: SNMP is used to manage network equipment, and SNMPv1/v2 uses unprotected community strings. If SNMP monitoring is not required, the service should be removed.
rules.impact: SNMP v1/v2 with the default community strings ('public', 'private') allows unauthorized reading of system configuration and status. SNMPv2 can also be used for denial-of-service attacks.

rules.title: The telnet server services are not in use
rules.explanation: The telnetd package contains the telnet daemon, which accepts user connections from other systems over the unencrypted telnet protocol. If remote administration over telnet is not required, the package should be removed and the service stopped and masked.
rules.impact: The telnet protocol transmits data, including credentials, in cleartext. An attacker with access to network traffic can capture logins and passwords and gain full control of the system.

rules.title: The tftp server services are not in use
rules.explanation: TFTP is a simplified file-transfer protocol without authentication, used to boot an operating system over the network (PXE). On servers without PXE functionality, TFTP should be removed.
rules.impact: TFTP does not support authentication, so anyone on the network can read and write files. It can be used to steal data or to upload malicious configuration files.

rules.title: The web proxy server services are not in use
rules.explanation: Squid is an HTTP proxy. If proxy functionality is not required, Squid should be removed so it does not provide an unauthorized path to the internet.
rules.impact: An unauthorized proxy lets users and malware bypass web-traffic controls and filtering. It can also be used for a covert outbound connection.

rules.title: The web server services are not in use
rules.explanation: The Apache2 and Nginx web servers should not run on hosts that are not meant to serve the web. Every unnecessary service expands the attack surface.
rules.impact: An unauthorized web server can expose internal data, become a vector for web attacks (SQLi, XSS, RFI), and serve as an entry point for further compromise of the network.

rules.title: The xinetd services are not in use
rules.explanation: xinetd is a super-server that controls the startup of other network services. It is obsolete and a significant security risk, and every service that depends on it becomes active as well.
rules.impact: xinetd manages many insecure legacy protocols (telnet, rsh, rlogin). Its presence means those protocols may be active and creates a single point of compromise.

rules.title: X window server services are not in use
rules.explanation: An X Window Server on a server means a graphical environment is present, which is not typical of production servers. Removing it reduces resource use and shrinks the attack surface.
rules.impact: X11 has a complex security model and has historically been subject to attacks over the X protocol. A graphical environment also greatly expands the attack surface and requires additional maintenance.

rules.title: The mail transfer agents are configured for local-only mode
rules.explanation: Mail transfer agents (MTAs), such as sendmail and Postfix, accept incoming mail and deliver it to users. If the system is not a mail server, the MTA should be configured to handle only local mail by limiting listening to 127.0.0.1.
rules.impact: MTAs are complex and have a long history of vulnerabilities. If the daemon listens on a network port, an attacker can use it for unauthorized mail relay, reconnaissance, or exploitation that compromises the system.

rules.title: Only approved services are listening on a network interface
rules.explanation: A listening network port is a port on which an application or process waits for incoming connections and acts as an endpoint for data exchange. Every open port must be justified: unnecessary services are stopped, and the packages that contain them are removed or masked.
rules.impact: Every listening service is a potential attack vector: a vulnerability in it lets an attacker gain access to the system or its data. Unaccounted and unnecessary services expand the attack surface and make perimeter control harder.
rules.scope: Listening sockets and owners from ss -plntu

rules.title: The nis client is not installed
rules.explanation: The NIS client obtains credentials from an NIS server over an unprotected channel. It is obsolete technology and should not be used on modern systems.
rules.impact: The NIS client sends credential queries without encryption. An attacker on the network can capture NIS traffic and obtain the password hashes of every user in the domain.

rules.title: The rsh client is not installed
rules.explanation: rsh is an obsolete protocol for remote command execution without encryption and should be fully replaced by SSH. An rsh client creates a risk that it will be used by accident.
rules.impact: rsh transmits data and commands in cleartext. Using rsh lets an attacker intercept the session and run arbitrary commands as the user.

rules.title: The talk client is not installed
rules.explanation: talk is an obsolete utility for text conversation between users of a system. It transmits data in cleartext and is not used in modern environments.
rules.impact: talk transmits messages without encryption, so a conversation can be intercepted. On servers, any unnecessary communication tools should be removed to minimize the attack surface.

rules.title: The telnet client is not installed
rules.explanation: Telnet transmits all data, including passwords, in cleartext. It has been fully replaced by SSH and should be removed from any modern system.
rules.impact: Even the telnet client creates risk: a user may connect to an insecure host and send credentials in cleartext. An attacker on the network can capture those credentials.

rules.title: The ldap client is not installed
rules.explanation: The LDAP client (ldap-utils) is not needed on systems that do not query a directory. Its presence can make reconnaissance of the LDAP infrastructure easier.
rules.impact: With an LDAP client, an attacker who has gained access to the system can easily query the LDAP directory for account information and the structure of the organization.

rules.title: The ftp client is not installed
rules.explanation: The FTP client transmits credentials in cleartext; file transfer should use SFTP. Removing the FTP client removes the risk that it will be used unintentionally.
rules.impact: Using the FTP client to transfer data lets an attacker capture credentials in cleartext. The presence of an FTP client also increases the risk of accidental insecure data transfer.

rules.title: The time synchronization is in use
rules.explanation: Time synchronization provides one time scale across all systems and is used by security mechanisms, logging, and audit tools. Depending on the environment, chrony, systemd-timesyncd, or ntp is used, and the chosen solution must be installed and running.
rules.impact: When clocks are out of sync, timestamps in logs from different systems cannot be matched, which hinders event correlation and forensic analysis. Incorrect time also breaks Kerberos, certificates, and other time-sensitive mechanisms.

rules.title: A single time synchronization daemon is in use
rules.explanation: Accurate time synchronization is critical for Kerberos, TLS certificates, audit logs, and distributed systems. Exactly one NTP daemon must be running.
rules.impact: Clock skew breaks Kerberos authentication (a tolerance of ±5 minutes), makes timestamps in logs unreliable for incident investigation, and can cause problems with TLS certificates.

rules.title: The systemd-timesyncd configured with authorized timeserver
rules.explanation: systemd-timesyncd should synchronize only with authorized NTP servers. Using unauthorized servers can lead to manipulation of the system time.
rules.impact: Synchronization with an unauthorized NTP server lets an attacker manipulate the system time, which breaks authentication, log correlation, and the operation of certificates.

rules.title: The systemd-timesyncd is enabled and running
rules.explanation: If systemd-timesyncd is selected as the NTP client, it must be running and enabled at boot. Stopping time synchronization disrupts services that depend on it.
rules.impact: Without time synchronization the system clock drifts, which breaks Kerberos authentication, makes timestamps in logs unreliable, and can cause TLS failures.

rules.title: The chrony is configured
rules.explanation: chrony is configured with the server and pool directives in chrony.conf. The server directive names a specific NTP server the client synchronizes from, and the pool directive names a pool that resolves to several addresses; both directives may be specified more than once.
rules.impact: If chrony uses untrustworthy or unauthorized time sources, an attacker can falsify the system time. That breaks logging, authentication, and mechanisms that depend on consistent timestamps.

rules.title: The chrony is running as user _chrony
rules.explanation: Running chronyd as the unprivileged user _chrony limits the damage if it is compromised. The principle of least privilege should be applied to every system daemon.
rules.impact: Running chronyd as root means that compromising it through a vulnerability in the NTP protocol gives an attacker full superuser privileges.

rules.title: The chrony is enabled and running
rules.explanation: chrony must be active and enabled to start at boot when it is the selected NTP client. That keeps time synchronization continuous across reboots.
rules.impact: A non-running NTP client lets the system clock drift, which breaks PKI (outdated certificates), Kerberos authentication, and correlation of security events in the logs.

rules.title: The cron daemon is enabled and active
rules.explanation: The cron daemon runs scheduled tasks, including system maintenance and audit jobs. It must be active so that critical system jobs run.
rules.impact: A non-running cron can skip log rotation, updates of security databases (ClamAV, fail2ban), and filesystem integrity checks (AIDE).

rules.title: The access to /etc/crontab is configured
rules.explanation: The file /etc/crontab is used by the cron service to manage system jobs. Permissions require the owner user and group to be root, and only the owner may read or write the file.
rules.impact: Write access to /etc/crontab lets an unprivileged user add a job that runs as root and escalate privileges. Read access discloses information about system jobs and helps plan an attack.

rules.title: The access to /etc/cron.hourly is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.hourly directory holds system cron jobs that run hourly; files in it are edited by an administrator by hand, not with the crontab command. Permissions limit read, write, and search to the root user and the root group.
rules.impact: Write access to the directory lets an unprivileged user run arbitrary code as root and escalate privileges. Read access discloses privilege-escalation methods and makes it possible to bypass audit controls.

rules.title: The access to /etc/cron.daily is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.daily directory holds system cron jobs that run daily; an administrator manages the files by hand, not with the crontab command. Permissions limit read, write, and search to the root user and the root group, keeping the directory closed to ordinary users.
rules.impact: With write access, an unprivileged user can place a job in the directory that runs as root and escalate privileges. Read access discloses information about system jobs that is useful for bypassing audit.

rules.title: The access to /etc/cron.weekly is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.weekly directory holds system cron jobs that run once a week; files in it are edited by the system administrator by hand. Permissions limit read, write, and search to the root user and the root group.
rules.impact: Write access to this directory lets an unprivileged user insert a job that will run as root and gain elevated privileges. Read access reveals system jobs and ways to bypass controls.

rules.title: The access to /etc/cron.monthly is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.monthly directory holds system cron jobs that run once a month; files in it are edited by an administrator by hand, not with the crontab command. Permissions limit read, write, and search to the root user and the root group.
rules.impact: Write access to the directory gives an unprivileged user a way to run arbitrary commands as root and escalate privileges. Read access discloses the contents of system jobs and makes it easier to prepare an attack.

rules.title: The access to /etc/cron.yearly is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.yearly directory holds system cron jobs that run once a year; files in it are edited by an administrator directly, not with the crontab command. Permissions limit read, write, and search to the root user only.
rules.impact: Write access for unprivileged users lets them insert arbitrary commands that run yearly as root, providing a path to privilege escalation. Read access discloses job contents and sensitive information about the system.

rules.title: The access to /etc/cron.d is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.d directory holds system cron jobs with a more flexible schedule than jobs in /etc/crontab; files in it are edited by an administrator by hand. Permissions limit read, write, and search to the root user and the root group.
rules.impact: Write access to /etc/cron.d lets an unprivileged user register a job that runs as root and escalate privileges. Read access discloses the schedule of system jobs and helps bypass audit controls.

rules.title: The access to crontab is configured
rules.explanation: The crontab command installs, removes, and views the cron daemon job tables. The files /etc/cron.allow and /etc/cron.deny decide who may use it, and /etc/cron.allow takes priority when both exist; the files must be readable by everyone or by the crontab group.
rules.impact: If access to crontab is not limited by an allow list, any user can schedule jobs, including for persistence and privilege escalation. A deny list is easy to forget to update when a new account is created, which leaves a gap.

rules.title: The access to at is configured
rules.explanation: The at command defers a job until a specified time, and batch defers it until a period of low load. The files /etc/at.allow and /etc/at.deny decide who may schedule such jobs; when /etc/at.allow exists, only the users listed in it are allowed.
rules.impact: Without an access restriction, any user can schedule deferred execution of commands, including for persistence and privilege escalation. A deny list requires manual maintenance and easily becomes incomplete when new accounts appear.

rules.title: IPv6 status is identified
rules.explanation: IPv6 is the current version of the IP protocol, with 128-bit addressing, hierarchical routing, quality-of-service support, and automatic configuration. Whether IPv6 is used in the infrastructure must be determined, so that the corresponding guidance is applied or the protocol is disabled.
rules.impact: If IPv6 is not used but remains enabled, traffic can bypass firewall rules and monitoring that cover only IPv4. That creates a hidden channel for attacks and data leakage.

rules.title: The wireless interfaces are not available
rules.explanation: Wireless interfaces are used when a wired network is unavailable and are implemented by kernel modules loaded while the system is running. If wireless connectivity is not required, the corresponding kernel modules should be disabled.
rules.impact: A wireless interface can be used as a bypass network path to evade monitoring, exfiltrate data, or connect to a rogue access point while bypassing the perimeter. Disabling the modules reduces the attack surface.

rules.title: The bluetooth services are not in use
rules.explanation: Bluetooth is not used for production purposes on servers and creates an additional attack vector. The BlueZ stack has a history of serious vulnerabilities.
rules.impact: Bluetooth vulnerabilities (BlueBorne, BIAS, KNOB) allow remote code execution with no user interaction. Active Bluetooth on a server is a serious attack vector that needs no physical contact.

rules.title: The atm kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) is a network, data-link, and physical-layer protocol based on virtual channels and paths. It is usually unnecessary on servers and workstations, so the corresponding kernel module should be blocked.
rules.impact: If the atm module is loaded, an attacker can use flaws in its implementation to disrupt the system or execute code with kernel privileges. Disabling an unused protocol reduces the local attack surface.

rules.title: The can kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: CAN (Controller Area Network) is a serial communications protocol originally created for the automotive industry and also used in industry and medicine. If the protocol is not used, the can kernel module should be blocked.
rules.impact: A loaded can module allows flaws in the protocol implementation to be exploited, including for code execution with kernel privileges. On systems where CAN is not needed, that support adds an unnecessary attack surface.

rules.title: The dccp kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: DCCP (Datagram Congestion Control Protocol) is an experimental transport protocol that is unused in most environments. Disabling its module reduces the attack surface of the network stack.
rules.impact: Rarely used network modules have historically contained critical vulnerabilities. The dccp module had known security flaws that allowed code execution with kernel privileges.

rules.title: The rds kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: RDS (Reliable Datagram Sockets) is used in high-performance clusters (Oracle RAC). On standard servers this module is unnecessary and can be disabled.
rules.impact: RDS has a history of serious vulnerabilities (CVE-2010-3904 and others) that allowed local users to gain root privileges. Disabling it fully removes this vector.

rules.title: The sctp kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: SCTP (Stream Control Transmission Protocol) is a transport protocol for telephony networks. In most server environments it is unused and should be disabled.
rules.impact: SCTP support expands the network attack surface. Vulnerabilities in the SCTP implementation have allowed a kernel panic and arbitrary code execution in kernel space.

rules.title: The tipc kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: TIPC (Transparent Inter-Process Communication) is a protocol for clustered applications. If cluster software is not used, the module should be disabled to reduce the kernel code base.
rules.impact: Vulnerabilities in tipc (CVE-2022-0435 and others) allowed privilege escalation and code execution in kernel context. Disabling it removes this attack vector.

rules.title: The unneeded network protocol kernel modules are not available
rules.explanation: The Linux kernel ships dozens of network-protocol implementations as loadable modules (esp4, esp6, rxrpc, sctp, dccp, rds, tipc, appletalk, decnet, ipx, x25, rose, ax25, netrom, econet, llc), available under /lib/modules/. This recommendation sets a site policy: unused network modules are blocked in /etc/modprobe.d/ and bound to /bin/false, so the kernel refuses to load them.
rules.impact: Every loadable network module is reachable by an unprivileged user through sockets, autoload, or incoming traffic, and its code runs in the kernel. A security flaw, for example in esp4/esp6 fragmentation handling or in rxrpc RPC processing, can escalate privileges to root or cause a remote denial of service.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.ip_forward is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.ip_forward parameter determines whether the system can forward IPv4 packets between interfaces. On a host that does not act as a router, forwarding should be disabled.
rules.impact: If IPv4 forwarding is enabled, a system with several interfaces can be used as a transit node to reach internal networks, and information about the network topology spreads beyond the network.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.all.forwarding is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.conf.all.forwarding parameter controls IPv4 packet forwarding on all interfaces. The host itself is not a router, so forwarding should be disabled.
rules.impact: When forwarding is enabled, the host starts routing traffic between interfaces, which lets it be used to reach networks that should stay isolated and discloses information about the network topology.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.default.forwarding is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.conf.default.forwarding parameter controls IPv4 packet forwarding on newly added network interfaces. On a host that does not act as a router, forwarding should be disabled.
rules.impact: If forwarding is enabled, new interfaces immediately start routing traffic, which can open a path to internal networks and spread information about the network topology.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects parameter controls sending of IPv4 ICMP redirects on all interfaces. Such messages point other nodes to an alternative route, and a host that is not a router does not need to send them.
rules.impact: A compromised host can send false ICMP redirects to other routers, distorting routing and directing users to systems under an attacker's control.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.default.send_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.conf.default.send_redirects parameter controls sending of IPv4 ICMP redirects on newly added network interfaces. A host that is not a router does not need to send redirects.
rules.impact: When sending of redirects is enabled, a compromised host can send false ICMP redirects, distorting routing on the network and redirecting traffic to the attacker's systems.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.icmp_ignore_bogus_error_responses is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.icmp_ignore_bogus_error_responses parameter determines whether the kernel logs invalid responses that violate RFC-1122 and arrive in broadcast frames. Enabling the parameter disables that logging.
rules.impact: Some routers and attackers send responses that violate RFC-1122 in order to fill the log filesystem with many useless messages and push out useful records.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts parameter determines whether ICMP echo and timestamp requests addressed to broadcast and multicast addresses are ignored. This reduces the risk that the host will participate in amplification attacks.
rules.impact: If the host answers broadcast ICMP requests, it can be drawn into a Smurf attack: many nodes send replies to a spoofed source address and multiply the volume of traffic.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects parameter controls acceptance of IPv4 ICMP redirects on all interfaces. Such messages allow an external device to change the system's routing table, so accepting them should be disabled.
rules.impact: If redirects are accepted, an external node can change the system's routing tables and redirect traffic through a device controlled by an attacker.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects parameter controls acceptance of IPv4 ICMP redirects on newly added network interfaces. Disabling acceptance stops external devices from changing the system's routing through those interfaces.
rules.impact: If acceptance of redirects is allowed, new interfaces accept routing changes from external devices, which can direct traffic through the attacker's system.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.all.secure_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: Secure ICMP redirects differ from ordinary ones only in that they come from gateways listed in the default gateway list. The net.ipv4.conf.all.secure_redirects parameter controls acceptance of them on all interfaces.
rules.impact: Even a known gateway can be compromised. If secure redirects are accepted, that gateway can change the system's routing table and redirect its traffic.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.default.secure_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: Secure ICMP redirects come from gateways listed in the default gateway list. The net.ipv4.conf.default.secure_redirects parameter controls acceptance of them on newly added network interfaces.
rules.impact: A compromised default gateway can, through new interfaces, change the system's routing table and send traffic into a network controlled by an attacker.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter parameter enables reverse-path filtering for IPv4 traffic on all interfaces. The check tests whether the source address of an incoming packet is reachable through the same interface and drops packets whose source is unreachable.
rules.impact: Without reverse-path filtering, an attacker can send the system packets with spoofed source addresses, including for amplification attacks. With asymmetric routing, enabling the parameter can disrupt network operation.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter parameter enables reverse-path filtering for IPv4 traffic on newly added network interfaces. Packets whose source address is not reachable through the receiving interface are dropped.
rules.impact: Without reverse-path filtering on new interfaces, an attacker can send packets with spoofed source addresses. With asymmetric routing, enabling the parameter can disrupt network operation.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route parameter determines whether IPv4 packets with the Strict Source Route or Loose Source Routing option set are accepted on all interfaces. Source routing lets the sender choose the packet path.
rules.impact: If source routing is allowed, an attacker can specify a path that bypasses normal routing and reach isolated systems that use private addresses.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route parameter determines whether IPv4 packets with the SSR or LSR options are accepted on newly added network interfaces. Source routing lets the sender choose the packet path.
rules.impact: If source routing is allowed, an attacker can set an arbitrary route through new interfaces and reach systems with private addresses that normal routing cannot reach.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians parameter turns on kernel logging of IPv4 packets with non-routable source addresses received on any interface. This helps detect spoofing of source addresses.
rules.impact: Without logging of such packets, an administrator will not see attempts to send spoofed packets, which makes source-address spoofing attacks harder to detect.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.default.log_martians is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.conf.default.log_martians parameter turns on kernel logging of IPv4 packets with non-routable source addresses received on newly added network interfaces.
rules.impact: If logging is disabled, attempts to send spoofed packets to new interfaces will go unnoticed, which makes incident investigation harder.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies parameter enables SYN cookies. Until the half-open connection queue is full the kernel handles SYN packets in the normal way, and it then replies with a SYN/ACK that carries a specially formed sequence number, so legitimate connections can still be accepted when the queue overflows.
rules.impact: In a SYN flood the attacker sends many SYN packets without completing the three-way handshake, quickly exhausts the half-open connection queue, and blocks legitimate connections from being established.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.all.route_localnet is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.conf.all.route_localnet parameter allows 127/8 addresses to be used for local routing and tells the system not to treat loopback addresses as martian when routing. Disabling the parameter prevents traffic from external interfaces from being routed to loopback addresses.
rules.impact: If the parameter is enabled, traffic from external interfaces can be routed to loopback addresses, which breaks network isolation and opens access to local services.

rules.title: The net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding parameter determines whether the system can forward IPv6 packets; on a host that is not a router, forwarding should be disabled. If IPv6 is disabled or the system is a router, this recommendation does not apply.
rules.impact: If IPv6 forwarding is enabled, a system with several interfaces can route IPv6 traffic, which discloses the network topology and lets the host be used as a transit node.

rules.title: The net.ipv6.conf.default.forwarding is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv6.conf.default.forwarding parameter determines whether the system can forward IPv6 packets on the default interface and on newly added interfaces. On a host that is not a router, forwarding should be disabled.
rules.impact: When forwarding is enabled, new interfaces immediately start routing IPv6 traffic, which lets the host be used to reach isolated networks and discloses topology information.

rules.title: The net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects parameter controls acceptance of IPv6 ICMP redirects on all interfaces. Such messages allow an external device to change the system's routing, so accepting them should be disabled.
rules.impact: If IPv6 redirects are accepted, an external device can change the system's routing tables and redirect traffic through a node controlled by an attacker.

rules.title: The net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_redirects parameter controls acceptance of IPv6 ICMP redirects on newly added network interfaces. Disabling acceptance stops external devices from changing the system's routing through those interfaces.
rules.impact: If acceptance of IPv6 redirects is allowed, new interfaces accept routing changes from external devices, which can direct traffic through the attacker's system.

rules.title: The net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route parameter determines whether IPv6 packets with the SSR or LSR options set are accepted on all interfaces. Source routing lets the sender specify the packet path in part or in full.
rules.impact: If source routing is allowed, an attacker can set an arbitrary path and reach isolated networks while bypassing normal routing.

rules.title: The net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_source_route is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_source_route parameter determines whether IPv6 packets with the SSR or LSR options are accepted on newly added network interfaces. Source routing lets the sender choose the packet path.
rules.impact: If source routing is allowed, an attacker can set an arbitrary route through new interfaces and reach systems that normal routing cannot reach.

rules.title: The net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_ra is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_ra parameter controls acceptance of IPv6 Router Advertisement messages on any network device. Routers send these messages periodically so hosts can configure themselves automatically, but accepting them allows an unwanted route to be imposed on the system.
rules.impact: If the system accepts Router Advertisement messages, an attacker can impose a false default route and redirect traffic through a compromised node.
