rules.title: The net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_ra is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_ra parameter controls acceptance of IPv6 Router Advertisement messages on newly added network devices. Accepting these messages allows the host routing to be reconfigured automatically from outside.
rules.impact: If new interfaces accept Router Advertisement messages, an attacker can impose a false route on the system and redirect traffic through a node under the attacker's control.

rules.title: The ufw is installed
rules.explanation: UFW (Uncomplicated Firewall) is the standard utility for managing iptables on Ubuntu. It must be installed to enforce a host traffic-filtering policy.
rules.impact: Without an installed firewall, the server has no host-based control of incoming connections. Any network service started on the server immediately becomes reachable from the network without restriction.

rules.title: The ufw service is configured
rules.explanation: The ufw.service service manages the UFW firewall and is responsible for applying and maintaining filter rules for incoming and outgoing traffic. It must be enabled and running, and rules for required services, such as SSH, should be added before the firewall is enabled.
rules.impact: If the ufw service is not running, firewall rules are not applied and the system stays open to any network traffic. Before enabling it, confirm that a rule for SSH has been added, or access to the host may be lost.

rules.title: The ufw incoming default is configured
rules.explanation: The default policy for incoming traffic determines whether connections from external sources are allowed without separate UFW rules. Incoming connections should be denied by default.
rules.impact: Under an accept policy, the firewall allows any packet that has no deny rule. Allowing known acceptable use is simpler and safer than listing everything that is forbidden.

rules.title: The ufw outgoing default is configured
rules.explanation: The default policy for outgoing traffic determines whether server applications and services can open connections to external networks without separate UFW rules. A strict deny policy requires an explicit allow for each necessary destination.
rules.impact: If outgoing traffic uses an accept policy, any compromised application can open connections to external nodes without restriction, which makes data exfiltration and payload download easier.

rules.title: The ufw routed default is configured
rules.explanation: The default policy for routed traffic determines whether UFW forwards traffic between network interfaces without separate rules. Such forwarding should be denied or disabled.
rules.impact: If routed traffic is allowed, the system can forward packets between network interfaces, which creates a path for unwanted or malicious traffic into protected network segments.

rules.title: The access to /etc/ssh/sshd_config is configured
rules.explanation: /etc/ssh/sshd_config is the main configuration file of the OpenSSH server (sshd), which serves secure remote logins; includable sshd drop-in files are placed in the same directory by default. This setting defines the owner of the file and the permissions on it.
rules.impact: If the sshd configuration file is available to unprivileged users, they can change SSH server settings and weaken protection of remote access, to the point of gaining unauthorized access to the system.

rules.title: The access to /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ directory is configured
rules.explanation: /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ is the directory of includable sshd configuration; the Include directive in the main file processes every *.conf file in it. This setting defines the owner of the directory and the access mode on it.
rules.impact: With mode 0755, any local user can list the directory and read the drop-in files, exposing SSH server policy and details of groups, listen addresses, and key paths. That simplifies reconnaissance before privilege escalation.

rules.title: The access to SSH private host key files is configured
rules.explanation: An SSH private key is one of the two files used for public-key authentication, and possession of it proves the party's identity. This setting restricts access to the host private key files.
rules.impact: If an attacker obtains the host private key file, they can impersonate that host, subvert client trust, and carry out man-in-the-middle attacks.

rules.title: The access to SSH public host key files is configured
rules.explanation: An SSH public key is one of the two files used for public-key authentication and is used to verify digital signatures created by the matching private key. This setting restricts access to those files.
rules.impact: If an unprivileged user changes the host public key file, trust in the SSH server is undermined: clients may accept a forged key and connect to a host controlled by the attacker.

rules.title: The sshd access is configured
rules.explanation: The AllowUsers, AllowGroups, DenyUsers, or DenyGroups directives restrict which users are permitted SSH access. This applies least privilege for remote login.
rules.impact: Without an explicit user restriction, every system account, including service accounts, has SSH access. Compromise of any account allows remote login and further persistence.

rules.title: The sshd Banner is configured
rules.explanation: The SSH banner is displayed before authentication. It should contain a legal warning about authorized access, which is a standard compliance and legal requirement.
rules.impact: The absence of an authorized-access warning weakens the organization's legal position during incidents, because an attacker can claim they did not know unauthorized access was prohibited.

rules.title: The sshd Ciphers are configured
rules.explanation: SSH should use only modern, cryptographically strong ciphers. Obsolete algorithms (3DES, RC4, CBC mode) are vulnerable to known attacks and should be excluded.
rules.impact: Use of obsolete ciphers (3DES-CBC, arcfour) allows an attacker who can intercept traffic to decrypt the SSH session. That compromises all transmitted data and credentials.

rules.title: The sshd ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax are configured
rules.explanation: SSH session timeouts detect a dropped connection and terminate idle sessions. This prevents a buildup of abandoned sessions and reduces the risk that they will be hijacked.
rules.impact: Without timeouts, SSH sessions left open indefinitely can be hijacked by an attacker who gains access to the terminal. They also consume resources and make auditing of active connections harder.

rules.title: The sshd DisableForwarding is enabled
rules.explanation: DisableForwarding turns off every form of SSH tunneling: X11, port forwarding, and agent forwarding. On servers that do not need tunneling, this substantially reduces the attack surface.
rules.impact: SSH tunneling lets an attacker create covert channels through SSH to bypass the firewall and traffic-control systems. X11 forwarding also opens a path for attacks on the local X server.

rules.title: The sshd GSSAPIAuthentication is disabled
rules.explanation: GSSAPI authentication (Kerberos) is used only in environments with Active Directory. On servers without Kerberos, this mechanism should be disabled to simplify configuration and reduce risk.
rules.impact: Leaving GSSAPI authentication active without a Kerberos infrastructure can cause connection delays and potential attacks against the GSSAPI mechanism. Vulnerabilities in the GSSAPI implementation can be used to bypass authentication.

rules.title: The sshd HostbasedAuthentication is disabled
rules.explanation: Host-based authentication trusts the remote host without verifying the user. It is an archaic and insecure method that has been fully replaced by key-based authentication.
rules.impact: Host-based authentication allows passwordless login to the server from trusted hosts. Compromise of any trusted host gives an attacker immediate access without further authentication.

rules.title: The sshd IgnoreRhosts is enabled
rules.explanation: The IgnoreRhosts parameter prohibits use of .rhosts and .shosts files for authentication. Those are obsolete mechanisms without encryption, and they create serious vulnerabilities.
rules.impact: .rhosts files allow passwordless login from a specified host. An attacker who spoofs the trusted host's IP address, or who has compromised that host, gains immediate access without authentication.

rules.title: The sshd KexAlgorithms is configured
rules.explanation: Key-exchange (KEX) algorithms determine how the session key is established. Weak algorithms (DH group1, group14 with SHA1) are vulnerable to discrete-logarithm attacks.
rules.impact: Use of weak KEX algorithms exposes SSH session setup to cryptographic attacks. An adversary with sufficient computing resources can recover the session key and decrypt the traffic.

rules.title: The sshd post-quantum cryptography key exchange algorithms are configured
rules.explanation: OpenSSH supports post-quantum cryptography (PQC) to protect SSH connections against attacks by future quantum computers, using hybrid key-agreement algorithms. This setting defines the list of allowed key-exchange algorithms.
rules.impact: Without hybrid post-quantum algorithms, SSH traffic remains vulnerable to a harvest-now, decrypt-later attack: captured sessions can be decrypted once sufficiently powerful quantum computers exist.

rules.title: The sshd LoginGraceTime is configured
rules.explanation: LoginGraceTime sets the time allowed to complete authentication. A small value (30-60 seconds) prevents incomplete connections from being held open for attacks.
rules.impact: A large or zero LoginGraceTime lets an attacker hold many incomplete connections and consume server resources (DoS). It also widens the window for slow password-guessing attacks.

rules.title: The sshd LogLevel is configured
rules.explanation: The SSH log level (VERBOSE or INFO) controls how much detail is recorded for authentication events. Detailed logs are needed to detect attacks and investigate incidents.
rules.impact: Insufficient SSH logging makes it impossible to detect password-guessing attacks, unauthorized logins, and unusual activity. This critically reduces the ability to detect intrusions.

rules.title: The sshd MACs are configured
rules.explanation: MAC algorithms protect the integrity of SSH traffic. Obsolete algorithms (HMAC-MD5, HMAC-SHA1) are vulnerable to collision attacks and should be excluded from the configuration.
rules.impact: Use of weak MAC algorithms (MD5, SHA1) allows an attacker with access to the traffic to modify SSH packets without detection. This breaks the integrity of transmitted data and commands.

rules.title: The sshd MaxAuthTries is configured
rules.explanation: MaxAuthTries limits the number of authentication attempts in one connection. A value of no more than 4 prevents effective password guessing through a single connection.
rules.impact: Without a limit on authentication attempts, an attacker can perform unlimited password guessing within a single SSH connection. This significantly speeds up brute-force attacks.

rules.title: The sshd MaxSessions is configured
rules.explanation: MaxSessions limits the number of simultaneous sessions over one SSH connection. A reasonable limit (no more than 10) prevents abuse of multiplexing.
rules.impact: Without a MaxSessions limit, an unlimited number of sessions can be opened over one connection, which creates a DoS vector and makes auditing of active connections and sessions harder.

rules.title: The sshd MaxStartups is configured
rules.explanation: MaxStartups limits the number of unauthenticated incoming connections. Without that limit, an attacker can exhaust connections and block access for legitimate users.
rules.impact: Without a MaxStartups limit, an attacker can open thousands of incomplete connections and cause a denial of service for SSH. This denies administrators remote access to the server.

rules.title: The sshd PermitEmptyPasswords is disabled
rules.explanation: Disabling empty passwords ensures that accounts without a password cannot authenticate over SSH. Accounts with an empty password are a critical vulnerability.
rules.impact: Allowing empty passwords means any account without a password set is reachable over SSH without authentication. An attacker can log in immediately, even without knowing the username.

rules.title: The sshd PermitRootLogin is disabled
rules.explanation: Prohibiting direct SSH login as root is a fundamental security requirement. Administrators should log in under their own accounts and use sudo to elevate privileges.
rules.impact: If root login over SSH is allowed, a successful password guess or a stolen key immediately gives an attacker full control of the system. Logging also does not distinguish between administrators.

rules.title: The sshd PermitUserEnvironment is disabled
rules.explanation: PermitUserEnvironment allows users to set environment variables through ~/.ssh/environment. This can be used to bypass PATH restrictions and other security controls.
rules.impact: Through ~/.ssh/environment, an attacker with access to the home directory can set LD_PRELOAD, PATH, and other variables, which allows controls to be bypassed and arbitrary code to be executed.

rules.title: The sshd UsePAM is enabled
rules.explanation: PAM provides centralized and extensible SSH authentication. Enabling UsePAM allows password policies, login-time restrictions, and two-factor authentication to be applied.
rules.impact: Without UsePAM, SSH bypasses PAM, so password policies, account restrictions (pam_faillock), and MFA cannot be applied. Authentication security is substantially reduced.

rules.title: The sudo is installed
rules.explanation: sudo is the standard privilege-elevation mechanism on Linux. Without it, users must work directly as root or use su, which reduces control and auditability.
rules.impact: Without sudo, administrators log in directly as root, which makes individual auditing of actions impossible. Privileges also cannot be separated among different administrative roles.

rules.title: The sudo commands use pty
rules.explanation: The use_pty parameter requires privileged commands to run in a pseudo-terminal. This prevents background processes from being started with sudo privileges and blocks a class of signal-based attacks.
rules.impact: Without use_pty, a malicious script invoked through sudo can start background processes that remain after the sudo session ends. This is a path for covert persistence on the system.

rules.title: The sudo log file exists
rules.explanation: A dedicated sudo log file records every privileged command together with the user, the command, and the time. This is critical for auditing and incident investigation.
rules.impact: Without dedicated sudo logging, actions performed with elevated privileges may go untracked. During incident investigation it is then impossible to determine who ran privileged commands and when.

rules.title: The users must provide password for escalation
rules.explanation: The operating system must require the user to enter a password when elevating privileges, for example when using sudo. This setting prevents privileged commands from running without re-authentication.
rules.impact: Without re-authentication, anyone who gains access to an unlocked session or terminal can perform privileged operations and reach resources they are not authorized to use.

rules.title: The re-authentication for privilege escalation is not disabled globally
rules.explanation: The global !authenticate flag in sudoers disables authentication for all users. This completely undermines the sudo security mechanism.
rules.impact: Globally disabling sudo authentication means any user can obtain root privileges without entering a password. Compromise of any user session then leads immediately to full system compromise.

rules.title: The sudo timestamp_timeout is configured
rules.explanation: The sudo timestamp_timeout parameter defines how long sudo privileges remain active after the first successful password entry. This setting limits that interval to a reasonable value.
rules.impact: An excessively large or infinite timeout widens the window in which an attacker who gains access to an unlocked user terminal can run privileged commands without entering a password.

rules.title: The access to the su command is restricted
rules.explanation: The su command runs a command or shell as another user and has largely been replaced by the more controllable sudo. Uncommenting pam_wheel.so in /etc/pam.d/su allows su only for members of a specific group, which should remain empty.
rules.impact: If su is allowed for every user, an attacker can bypass sudo control and auditing and elevate privileges without restriction, while the escalation goes unnoticed.

rules.title: The latest version of pam is installed
rules.explanation: A current version of PAM (libpam-runtime) contains security fixes and support for modern authentication methods. Outdated versions may contain known vulnerabilities.
rules.impact: An outdated PAM may still contain vulnerabilities, already fixed in later versions, that allow authentication to be bypassed. PAM is a central security component, and its vulnerabilities directly affect login protection.

rules.title: The latest version of libpam-modules is installed
rules.explanation: libpam-modules contains the standard PAM modules (pam_unix, pam_limits, pam_env). Without them, basic Linux authentication is impossible, so the package is a required system component.
rules.impact: Missing libpam-modules means the standard PAM modules are absent, which makes user authentication impossible. The system then becomes either completely inaccessible or insecure because access control is missing.

rules.title: The latest version of libpam-pwquality is installed
rules.explanation: libpam-pwquality provides the pam_pwquality module for checking password quality. Without it, a password-complexity policy cannot be applied through PAM.
rules.impact: Without libpam-pwquality, a password-complexity policy cannot be applied. Users can set trivial passwords that are easy to guess or brute-force.

rules.title: The latest version of cracklib-runtime is installed
rules.explanation: The cracklib-runtime package enables the cracklib2 password-checking library. This setting requires a current version of that package.
rules.impact: An outdated cracklib-runtime may lack the latest security fixes, allowing weak-password checks to be defeated or bypassed and accounts to be compromised.

rules.title: The pam_unix module is enabled
rules.explanation: pam_unix provides standard Unix authentication through /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow. It is the base module that must be active in the PAM authentication stack.
rules.impact: The absence of pam_unix from the PAM stack breaks standard password authentication. Authentication may fail completely or be bypassed through another mechanism.

rules.title: The pam_faillock module is enabled
rules.explanation: pam_faillock locks an account after a configured number of failed login attempts. This is PAM-level protection against brute-force attacks.
rules.impact: Without pam_faillock, there is no limit on failed login attempts. An attacker can perform unlimited password guessing through su, login, and other PAM services with no risk of lockout.

rules.title: The pam_pwquality module is enabled
rules.explanation: pam_pwquality applies password-complexity policy when a password is changed. Without this module in the PAM stack, the settings in /etc/security/pwquality.conf are not applied.
rules.impact: Without pam_pwquality in the PAM stack, users can set passwords of any strength. Weak passwords are easy to guess or crack, which makes unauthorized access easier.

rules.title: The pam_pwhistory module is enabled
rules.explanation: pam_pwhistory prevents reuse of recent passwords. Without it, users can immediately change a password back to the previous one and bypass rotation policy.
rules.impact: Without password-history control, a user can immediately change the password back to the previous one after a forced change. This completely undermines password-rotation policy.

rules.title: The password failed attempts lockout is configured
rules.explanation: The deny parameter in /etc/security/faillock.conf sets the number of failed login attempts before lockout. A value of no more than 5 is the standard for brute-force protection.
rules.impact: Without a limit on failed attempts, an attacker can perform unlimited password guessing. Weak passwords will be guessed in seconds, and stronger ones in hours, when no lockout is in place.

rules.title: The password unlock time is configured
rules.explanation: unlock_time sets how long an account stays locked after the number of failed attempts is exceeded. A value of at least 900 seconds (15 minutes) significantly reduces the effectiveness of brute force.
rules.impact: A short unlock time lets an attacker guess passwords systematically with brief pauses. A 15-minute lockout makes a full brute-force search practically infeasible.

rules.title: The password failed attempts lockout includes root account
rules.explanation: The even_deny_root parameter extends failed-attempt lockout to the root account. Without it, root remains unprotected against brute-force attacks on SSH and the console.
rules.impact: Without root lockout, an attacker can perform unlimited guessing of the root password. A successful guess of the root password means immediate and complete compromise of the system.

rules.title: The password number of changed characters is configured
rules.explanation: The difok parameter sets the minimum number of characters that must differ between the new password and the previous one. A value of 2 or more prevents minor changes (password1 > password2).
rules.impact: Without a required number of changed characters, a user can change only one character and keep essentially the same password. This bypasses rotation policy while retaining a weak password.

rules.title: The password length is configured
rules.explanation: The minlen parameter sets the minimum allowed length of a new password and cannot be less than 6. This setting defines how many characters a user password must contain.
rules.impact: Short passwords reduce the search space and leave the system vulnerable to brute-force and dictionary attacks, which can compromise accounts and allow unauthorized access.

rules.title: The password complexity is configured
rules.explanation: Password complexity is set in pam_pwquality by the parameters minclass, dcredit, ucredit, lcredit, and ocredit, which define the required number of character classes. This setting defines the composition requirements for new passwords.
rules.impact: Without complexity requirements, passwords stay predictable and vulnerable to dictionary and brute-force attacks, allowing an attacker to guess credentials and gain access to the system.

rules.title: The password same consecutive characters is configured
rules.explanation: maxrepeat limits the number of identical consecutive characters (for example, 'aaa'). This prevents use of trivial passwords made of repeated characters.
rules.impact: Without a limit on repeated characters, users create predictable passwords such as 'aaaaaa1!' or 'P@ssssword'. Those passwords are guessed within minutes by a dictionary attack.

rules.title: The password maximum sequential characters is configured
rules.explanation: maxsequence limits runs of consecutive keyboard characters (abc, 123, qwerty). This prevents predictable sequences from being used in passwords.
rules.impact: Passwords with long sequences (password123, qwerty789) are easy to guess from dictionaries. Without a maxsequence limit, users create predictable passwords despite their apparent complexity.

rules.title: The password dictionary check is enabled
rules.explanation: dictcheck in pwquality compares a password with a dictionary of common passwords. This prevents use of passwords that appear in attack dictionaries.
rules.impact: Without dictionary checking, a user can choose passwords from the top million (password, letmein, admin123). Those passwords are the first ones tried in brute-force attacks and credential stuffing.

rules.title: The password quality checking is enforced
rules.explanation: The enforce parameter in the pam_pwquality configuration ensures that password-quality requirements are mandatory and cannot be ignored.
rules.impact: Without mandatory enforcement, users can press Enter several times to skip weak-password warnings. Password-quality policy then becomes advisory rather than required.

rules.title: The password quality is enforced for the root user
rules.explanation: By default, pam_pwquality does not check the root password. enforce_for_root enables quality checking for the privileged account as well, which is a critical target.
rules.impact: A weak root password is a catastrophic vulnerability. Without enforce_for_root, an administrator can set a simple root password that immediately becomes the primary target of brute-force attacks.

rules.title: The password history remember is configured
rules.explanation: The remember parameter sets how many of the most recent passwords cannot be reused. A value of 5 or more prevents cyclic reuse of the same passwords.
rules.impact: Without history control, a user immediately returns to a preferred old password after a forced change. Password-rotation policy loses its purpose if the same password can be used again.

rules.title: The password history is enforced for the root user
rules.explanation: By default, pam_pwhistory does not apply to root. enforce_for_root extends the password-reuse restriction to the privileged account.
rules.impact: Without root password-history control, an administrator can immediately return to a compromised password after changing it. For root this is especially critical, given full access to the system.

rules.title: The pam_pwhistory includes use_authtok
rules.explanation: use_authtok in pam_pwhistory tells the module to use the password already entered by the previous module in the stack. Without this parameter, the module prompts for the password twice.
rules.impact: Without use_authtok, pam_pwhistory may operate on a different password than the other modules check, which makes validation inconsistent. This can cause authentication errors or incorrect application of policy.

rules.title: The pam_unix does not include nullok
rules.explanation: The nullok parameter in pam_unix allows passwordless login for accounts with an empty password field. This creates a critical vulnerability and must be explicitly disabled.
rules.impact: With nullok, any account that has no password set is accessible without authentication. An attacker can log in by simply pressing Enter at the password prompt.

rules.title: The pam_unix does not include remember
rules.explanation: The remember parameter in pam_unix is obsolete and has been replaced by pam_pwhistory. Its presence creates a conflict between two password-history mechanisms.
rules.impact: Using remember in pam_unix together with pam_pwhistory creates a conflict and unpredictable password-history behavior. One of the mechanisms can be bypassed.

rules.title: The pam_unix includes a strong password hashing algorithm
rules.explanation: pam_unix should use a strong password hashing algorithm (yescrypt, SHA-512, or bcrypt). Obsolete algorithms (MD5, DES) do not protect hashes adequately.
rules.impact: Weak hashing algorithms (MD5) allow a hash to be cracked in seconds on modern hardware. If /etc/shadow is disclosed, all passwords will be compromised within minutes.

rules.title: The pam_unix includes use_authtok
rules.explanation: use_authtok in pam_unix forces the module to use the token already obtained earlier in the PAM stack. This keeps password checking consistent across modules.
rules.impact: Without use_authtok, pam_unix may prompt for the password again, which causes inconsistency and can produce authentication errors. In the worst case, a state is created in which the password check is bypassed.

rules.title: The password expiration is configured
rules.explanation: PASS_MAX_DAYS in /etc/login.defs sets the maximum password lifetime. A value of 365 days or less ensures regular password rotation and limits the damage from compromise.
rules.impact: Without an expiration period, a password stays unchanged for years. A compromised password gives an attacker lasting access with no automatic way to revoke it.

rules.title: The minimum password days is configured
rules.explanation: The PASS_MIN_DAYS parameter sets the minimum number of days between password changes, and earlier change attempts are rejected. If the parameter is unset, the value 0 is used, which disables the restriction.
rules.impact: Without a limit on how often a password can be changed, users can change it repeatedly to bypass reuse controls and return to an old compromised password.

rules.title: The password expiration warning days is configured
rules.explanation: PASS_WARN_AGE defines how many days before expiration the user is warned. A value of 7 days or more gives enough time for a planned password change.
rules.impact: Without timely warnings, users can be caught off guard when a password expires and then be locked out. Unplanned lockouts often lead to unsafe recovery procedures.

rules.title: The strong password hashing algorithm is configured
rules.explanation: ENCRYPT_METHOD in /etc/login.defs selects the password hashing algorithm for new accounts. Yescrypt or SHA-512 provides sufficient hash strength.
rules.impact: Using MD5 or DES for hashing allows a password to be cracked in seconds with a GPU. If the password database is leaked, every hash can be recovered almost immediately on modern hardware.

rules.title: The inactive password lock is configured
rules.explanation: INACTIVE sets the number of days after password expiration before the account is locked. The default is stored in /etc/default/useradd and applied to new accounts, the actual value for each account is in /etc/shadow, and a range of 1-30 days deactivates abandoned accounts.
rules.impact: Accounts whose passwords have expired and that are not locked automatically remain on the system with stale, potentially weak passwords. Abandoned accounts are a common path for unauthorized access.

rules.title: All users last password change date is in the past
rules.explanation: The date of the last password change must not be in the future; that indicates tampering with /etc/shadow to bypass password-change policy.
rules.impact: A password-change date in the future means an attacker or a malicious process modified /etc/shadow to prevent a forced password change. This is a clear sign of compromise.

rules.title: The root is the only UID 0 account
rules.explanation: UID 0 grants full superuser privileges, and only the root account should have UID 0. Any other UID 0 account is a sign of compromise or of a configuration error.
rules.impact: An additional account with UID 0 provides full root access while bypassing monitoring and auditing. This is a classic way to create a backdoor account on a compromised system.

rules.title: The root is the only GID 0 account
rules.explanation: Only the root account should belong to group GID 0 (root). Any other user with GID 0 receives root-group privileges, which is a sign of compromise.
rules.impact: An account with GID 0 has root-group privileges. An attacker can create a backdoor account with GID 0 and obtain superuser group privileges without an explicit UID 0.

rules.title: The group root is the only GID 0 group
rules.explanation: Only the root group should have GID 0. Additional groups with GID 0 indicate tampering with /etc/group and are a sign that the system has been compromised.
rules.impact: An additional group with GID 0 grants its members root-group privileges. This is a classic way to create hidden privileged access on a compromised system.

rules.title: The root account access is controlled
rules.explanation: The root account should be locked (password LK) or have an invalid password so that direct root login is impossible. Root access should be obtained only through sudo.
rules.impact: An active root password creates a direct path for brute-force attacks on the console and over SSH. Locking the account forces use of sudo, which provides auditing and a second authentication.

rules.title: The root path integrity
rules.explanation: The root PATH must not contain the current directory (.) or empty elements. Every directory on PATH must be owned by root and must not be writable by other users.
rules.impact: A '.' entry in the root PATH lets an attacker place a malicious binary named like a standard command (ls, id) in the current directory. When that name is run as root, the planted file executes instead of the system command.

rules.title: The root user umask is configured
rules.explanation: A umask of 027 or 077 for root ensures that files it creates are not readable or writable by other users. This prevents accidental creation of world-readable files by root.
rules.impact: Without a strict umask, files created by root (configurations, keys, scripts) may be readable or writable by unprivileged users, which discloses confidential data.

rules.title: The system accounts do not have a valid login shell
rules.explanation: System accounts (UID < 1000, except root) are meant to run services, not to support interactive login. They should be assigned /sbin/nologin or /bin/false.
rules.impact: A system account with a valid shell can be used by an attacker to log in if its password is compromised or authentication is configured insecurely. That grants the privileges of the service.

rules.title: The accounts without a valid login shell are locked
rules.explanation: Accounts that use /sbin/nologin or /bin/false as their shell should be locked (password LK). This is a second layer of protection: even if the shell restriction is bypassed, password authentication will fail.
rules.impact: An account without a valid shell but with an active password can still authenticate through PAM services (su, SSH). Locking the password removes that path even if the shell has been replaced.

rules.title: The nologin is not listed in /etc/shells
rules.explanation: The file /etc/shells lists valid command interpreters. nologin is not an interactive shell and must not appear in that list, because its presence can create unwanted exceptions.
rules.impact: If nologin is listed in /etc/shells, some services (FTP, SFTP) can grant access to accounts whose shell is /sbin/nologin, which contradicts their purpose and creates an unauthorized access path.

rules.title: The default user shell timeout is configured
rules.explanation: The TMOUT variable sets how long a shell may stay idle before the session ends automatically. A value of 900 seconds or less prevents a buildup of abandoned terminal sessions.
rules.impact: Without a shell timeout, an abandoned terminal session stays active indefinitely. An attacker who gains physical access to the terminal, or who hijacks the session, can run commands without authentication.

rules.title: The default user umask is configured
rules.explanation: A umask of 027 or 077 in the global profiles (/etc/profile, /etc/bash.bashrc) ensures that new files are created without permissions for other users by default.
rules.impact: The default umask 022 lets every user read newly created files. Scripts, configurations, and data created accidentally with those permissions can disclose confidential information.

rules.title: The journald service is active
rules.explanation: systemd-journald is the primary log-collection daemon on Ubuntu 24.04. It must be running to collect system events, including security and authentication events.
rules.impact: Without a running journald, system logs are not collected. Security events, authentication failures, and user actions go unrecorded, which makes attack detection impossible.

rules.title: The systemd-journal-remote service is not in use
rules.explanation: systemd-journal-remote.socket accepts journals from remote hosts. If the server is not a centralized log collector, this service should be disabled to avoid unauthorized receipt of data.
rules.impact: An active journal-intake service on a host that is not meant for that role creates unnecessary network attack surface and can be used to inject forged log records.

rules.title: The journald is configured to send logs to rsyslog
rules.explanation: ForwardToSyslog=yes in journald forwards every journald event to rsyslog for unified processing. This is required when both systems are used together.
rules.impact: Without ForwardToSyslog, events from journald (systemd services, the kernel) never reach rsyslog and are not sent to a centralized log server. Some security events will then be unavailable to the SIEM.

rules.title: The journald log file access is configured
rules.explanation: journald creates journal files when they do not already exist. This setting defines the permissions applied to those newly created journal files.
rules.impact: If permissions on journal files are too broad, unprivileged users can read or change sensitive log data, which discloses information and corrupts the audit trail.

rules.title: The journald log file rotation is configured
rules.explanation: journald can rotate journal files regularly so they do not fill the system or become unmanageably large. Rotation is configured in /etc/systemd/journald.conf.
rules.impact: Without rotation configured, journals will fill the disk, which can cause a denial of service and the loss of audit records needed to investigate incidents.

rules.title: The journald Storage is configured
rules.explanation: The Storage=persistent parameter makes journald write journals to disk under /var/log/journal. Without it, journals are kept only in memory and are lost on reboot.
rules.impact: Without persistent storage, all systemd journals are lost on reboot. If an incident causes the system to restart, every preceding security event is permanently destroyed.

rules.title: The journald Compress is configured
rules.explanation: Compressing journald journals reduces the disk space they use, which allows logs to be kept for a longer period. That matters for retrospective analysis during incident investigation.
rules.impact: Without compression, journals use much more space and the retention period shrinks. An attack carried out more than a week earlier may no longer be on record because uncompressed journals were rotated away.

rules.title: The rsyslog is installed
rules.explanation: rsyslog is an extended syslog implementation that can filter, format, and send logs to remote servers. When rsyslog is used, it must be installed.
rules.impact: Without rsyslog, the system cannot use the traditional syslog mechanism to collect logs. That removes centralized log collection and forwarding to SIEM systems.

rules.title: The rsyslog service is enabled and active
rules.explanation: When rsyslog is the primary logging system, it must be running and enabled at boot. Stopping rsyslog interrupts collection of all system logs.
rules.impact: A stopped rsyslog service means system log collection stops completely. Security events, including unauthorized access attempts and attacker actions, go unrecorded.

rules.title: The rsyslog log file creation mode is configured
rules.explanation: $FileCreateMode 0640 ensures that log files created by rsyslog are readable only by root and the adm group. This protects the logs from being read by unprivileged users.
rules.impact: Without restricted permissions on log files, any local user can read authentication logs, sudo commands, and other sensitive information, which makes reconnaissance easier after an account is compromised.

rules.title: The rsyslog logging is configured
rules.explanation: The files /etc/rsyslog.conf and /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf define logging rules and decide which files receive messages of each class. This setting ensures that rsyslog records events correctly.
rules.impact: If the rsyslog configuration is incomplete or disabled, important security events such as failed login attempts and su invocations are not recorded, and an attack will go unnoticed.

rules.title: The rsyslog is configured to send logs to a remote log host
rules.explanation: rsyslog can send collected events to a remote logging host, which provides centralized log management. This setting enables that forwarding.
rules.impact: If logs are stored only locally, an attacker who gains root access can alter or delete them and hide traces of their activity.

rules.title: The rsyslog is not configured to receive logs from a remote client
rules.explanation: rsyslog should not accept logs over the network (imtcp/imudp) unless the server is a centralized log collector. Accepting incoming logs expands the attack surface.
rules.impact: Active intake of UDP/TCP logs opens a network port to incoming connections. This is a path for injecting forged log records and for denial of service by flooding logs from external sources.

rules.title: The logrotate is configured
rules.explanation: The system supports regular rotation of log files so they do not fill the disk or become unmanageably large. The file /etc/logrotate.d/rsyslog defines rotation rules for logs created by syslog or rsyslog.
rules.impact: Without configured log rotation, logs consume all disk space. That causes a denial of service, loss of audit records, and makes security-event analysis difficult.

rules.title: The rsyslog-gnutls is installed
rules.explanation: The rsyslog-gnutls package provides TLS support for rsyslog and allows encrypted syslog messages to be sent and received over the syslog-transport-tls protocol. The OpenSSL driver from the rsyslog-openssl package is an accepted alternative.
rules.impact: Traditional syslog transmits data in clear text, so anyone listening on the network can read log contents and learn details about the system and accounts.

rules.title: The rsyslog forwarding uses gtls
rules.explanation: Network stream drivers are the layer between rsyslogd components and the transport layer, and they provide ordered delivery, authentication, and confidentiality. DefaultNetstreamDriver must be set to gtls, or to ossl when OpenSSL is used.
rules.impact: If the stream driver is not set to gtls, forwarded syslog traffic is not encrypted and an attacker on the network can intercept or alter it.

rules.title: The rsyslog CA certificates are configured
rules.explanation: When logs are forwarded over TLS, rsyslog uses a certificate authority (CA) certificate to verify the remote server certificate. The path is set by the DefaultNetstreamDriverCAFile option in the rsyslog configuration.
rules.impact: Without a trusted CA certificate, log forwarding can proceed without verifying the server. That allows man-in-the-middle attacks that intercept, alter, or drop audit data.

rules.title: The access to all logfiles has been configured
rules.explanation: Every file in /var/log must have restrictive permissions: no more open than 640 for files and 750 for directories. This prevents unprivileged users from reading the logs.
rules.impact: Publicly accessible logs reveal usernames, activity timestamps, configuration errors, and other data that an attacker uses to plan an attack and escalate privileges.

rules.title: The auditd packages are installed
rules.explanation: auditd is the Linux kernel audit subsystem that records system calls and kernel-level events. Without it, full operating-system security auditing cannot be implemented.
rules.impact: Without auditd, critical kernel-level security events cannot be recorded: use of setuid programs, changes to configuration files, and unauthorized attempts to access system resources.

rules.title: The auditd service is enabled and active
rules.explanation: The auditd service must stay running and be enabled at boot. Stopping it interrupts collection of critical kernel-level security events.
rules.impact: A stopped auditd leaves the system without kernel auditing. Every attacker action after the service stops (file changes, privilege use, network connections) goes unrecorded.

rules.title: The auditing for processes that start prior to auditd is enabled
rules.explanation: The kernel parameter audit=1 enables auditing at the earliest stages of boot, before auditd starts. This records bootloader and system initialization events.
rules.impact: Without audit=1 in the kernel parameters, early boot events (init, systemd) are not recorded. An attacker who injected code into the initialization process stays invisible to the audit system.

rules.title: The audit_backlog_limit is configured
rules.explanation: The kernel audit subsystem uses a socket-buffer queue to store audit events. The kernel boot parameter audit_backlog_limit=N limits the size of that queue and defines behavior when it overflows.
rules.impact: If an audit event exceeds the configured queue limit, a failure occurs and auditd records are lost, so potentially malicious activity can go unnoticed.

rules.title: The audit log storage size is configured
rules.explanation: max_log_file sets the maximum size of one auditd log file in MB. A correct setting prevents both filling the disk and rotating so often that history is lost.
rules.impact: Without a configured log file size, audit data can fill the entire /var/log/audit partition and cause a denial of service. A size that is too small causes rotation and loss of older records needed for an investigation.

rules.title: The audit logs are not automatically deleted
rules.explanation: max_log_file_action=keep_logs prevents automatic deletion of old audit logs. Logs should be archived or rotated, but not destroyed automatically.
rules.impact: Automatic deletion of audit logs destroys evidence of past incidents. An attacker who stays undetected benefits when traces of their actions disappear over time.

rules.title: The system is disabled when audit logs are full
rules.explanation: When the audit log partition fills, the system must halt or switch to single-user mode. This prevents operation without auditing, which is critical for compliance requirements.
rules.impact: A system that keeps running without active auditing because the disk is full cannot record security events. An attacker can deliberately fill the disk to disable auditing and attack without obstruction.

rules.title: The system warns when audit logs are low on space
rules.explanation: space_left_action=email ensures a warning is sent to the administrator when free space falls to the threshold. This allows action before space runs out.
rules.impact: Without advance warning, the audit partition fills unexpectedly. The administrator has no time to act, and the system either stops or stops recording audit events.

rules.title: The modification of the /etc/sudoers file is collected
rules.explanation: An audit rule watches changes to /etc/sudoers and to files in /etc/sudoers.d, so changes to the scope of administrator privileges can be monitored. Audit records are tagged with the identifier scope.
rules.impact: Unrecorded changes in /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d can mean an unauthorized expansion of administrator privileges, allowing an attacker to persist on the system and hide their actions.

rules.title: The actions as another user are always logged
rules.explanation: Auditing execve on a UID or EUID change records every command run as another user (through sudo, su, or runuser). This is essential for attributing actions during investigations.
rules.impact: Without auditing user switches, it is impossible to determine which commands were run through sudo or su. An attacker can disguise their actions as those of a legitimate administrator, with no way to attribute them.

rules.title: The events that modify the sudo log file are collected
rules.explanation: Modification of the sudo log file is a clear sign of log forgery. Auditing changes to that file detects attempts to conceal privileged actions.
rules.impact: An attacker with root privileges can alter the sudo log to remove traces of their actions. Auditing the log file itself through inotify records that manipulation.

rules.title: The events that modify date and time information are collected
rules.explanation: The system calls adjtimex, settimeofday, stime, and clock_settime are used to change the system time. Auditing them helps detect attempts to manipulate log timestamps.
rules.impact: Changing the system time lets an attacker break log correlation and create a false event timeline. This is a classic technique for covering tracks during incident investigation.

rules.title: The events that modify sethostname and setdomainname are collected
rules.explanation: An audit rule watches the sethostname and setdomainname system calls and creates an audit record when they complete. This records changes to the system hostname and domain name.
rules.impact: An unauthorized change to the hostname or domain name can break security mechanisms that depend on those names, and it can go unnoticed when the change is not audited.

rules.title: The events that modify /etc/issue and /etc/issue.net are collected
rules.explanation: An audit rule watches changes to /etc/issue and /etc/issue.net, whose contents are displayed to users before login. This records any edits to the warning messages.
rules.impact: An attacker can place false information in /etc/issue or /etc/issue.net and trick users into revealing credentials or other confidential information.

rules.title: The events that modify /etc/hosts and /etc/hostname are collected
rules.explanation: An audit rule watches changes to /etc/hosts, which maps host names to IP addresses, and to /etc/hostname, which contains the system hostname.
rules.impact: An unrecorded change to /etc/hosts can indicate an attempt to substitute name-to-address mappings and direct users and processes to hosts the attacker controls.

rules.title: The events that modify the system's network environment are collected
rules.explanation: An audit rule watches changes to the system network environment: the file /etc/network/interfaces, the directory /etc/network/interfaces.d/, and the directory /etc/netplan/, which holds YAML configurations. This records edits to network settings.
rules.impact: Unrecorded changes to network interfaces or scripts can make the host unreachable, break network segmentation, or compromise the system.

rules.title: The events that modify /etc/NetworkManager directory are collected
rules.explanation: An audit rule watches changes to the /etc/NetworkManager/ directory, which stores NetworkManager configuration files and parameters. This records edits to network settings.
rules.impact: Unrecorded changes in the /etc/NetworkManager directory can mean an unauthorized network reconfiguration that leads to traffic interception or loss of host availability.

rules.title: The use of privileged commands are collected
rules.explanation: Every setuid and setgid program on the system must be watched through audit. Using them raises privileges and is a critical security event.
rules.impact: Without auditing privileged commands, an attacker can use setuid programs to escalate privileges and leave no record. Privilege escalation most often happens through such programs.

rules.title: The unsuccessful file access attempts are collected
rules.explanation: Auditing unsuccessful file-open attempts (EACCES, EPERM) helps detect filesystem reconnaissance and attempts to access protected data without authorization.
rules.impact: A series of file-access failures is a clear sign of reconnaissance or an attempt to bypass restrictions. Without auditing those events, an attacker can systematically enumerate accessible files and remain undetected.

rules.title: The events that modify /etc/group information are collected
rules.explanation: An audit rule watches events that change user and group information, including /etc/group, which holds the system groups. This records edits to group membership.
rules.impact: Unexpected changes in /etc/group can indicate system compromise: an attacker adds an account to a privileged group in order to expand rights and hide their activity.

rules.title: The events that modify /etc/passwd information are collected
rules.explanation: An audit rule watches events that change user and group information, including /etc/passwd, which holds the system accounts. This records edits to the user list.
rules.impact: Unexpected changes in /etc/passwd can indicate system compromise: an attacker creates or modifies accounts in order to persist and hide their activity.

rules.title: The events that modify /etc/shadow and /etc/gshadow are collected
rules.explanation: An audit rule watches events that change user and group information, including /etc/shadow, which holds user passwords, and /etc/gshadow, which holds group passwords. This records edits to those files.
rules.impact: Unexpected changes in /etc/shadow and /etc/gshadow can mean that an attacker replaced passwords or created hidden accounts in order to keep access to the system.

rules.title: The events that modify /etc/security/opasswd are collected
rules.explanation: An audit rule watches changes to /etc/security/opasswd, which stores old passwords when the corresponding PAM module is in use. This records edits to the history of previously used passwords.
rules.impact: Unexpected changes in /etc/security/opasswd can indicate an attempt to bypass password-reuse controls or to hide traces of account compromise.

rules.title: The events that modify /etc/nsswitch.conf file are collected
rules.explanation: An audit rule watches changes to /etc/nsswitch.conf, which defines the order in which databases and name-resolution mechanisms are used. This records edits to name-resolution and authentication configuration.
rules.impact: Unexpected changes in /etc/nsswitch.conf can indicate system compromise: an attacker redirects name resolution or authentication to a source they control and hides their activity.

rules.title: The events that modify /etc/pam.conf and /etc/pam.d/ information are collected
rules.explanation: The audit configuration watches events that modify /etc/pam.conf and the contents of /etc/pam.d/. The first file defines the authentication services in use and the order in which they are called; the second stores the PAM configuration for each application.
rules.impact: An unauthorized change to these files can indicate system compromise: an attacker can hide their activity or take control of accounts.

rules.title: The discretionary access control permission modification events chmod,fchmod,fchmodat,fchmodat2 are collected
rules.explanation: The audit configuration watches changes to file permissions, attributes, owner, and group. The system calls chmod, fchmod, fchmodat, and fchmodat2 are recorded with the perm_mod tag.
rules.impact: Without auditing these calls, an attacker can quietly weaken permissions on critical files and gain unauthorized access to data or alter it.

rules.title: The discretionary access control permission modification events chown,fchown,lchown,fchownat are collected
rules.explanation: The audit configuration watches changes of file owner and group ownership. The system calls chown, fchown, lchown, and fchownat are recorded with the perm_mod tag.
rules.impact: Without auditing, an attacker can quietly place critical files under the control of another user or group and gain access to protected data.

rules.title: The discretionary access control permission modification events setxattr,lsetxattr,fsetxattr,removexattr,lremovexattr,fremovexattr collected
rules.explanation: The audit configuration watches changes to extended file attributes. The system calls setxattr, lsetxattr, fsetxattr, removexattr, lremovexattr, and fremovexattr are recorded with the perm_mod tag.
rules.impact: Extended attributes can be used to hide data and bypass access restrictions, so without auditing those actions remain unnoticed.

rules.title: The successful file system mounts are collected
rules.explanation: Auditing successful filesystem mounts tracks attachment of external media and mounting of network resources, which is an important security event.
rules.impact: An unauthorized mount of external media or a network resource, if not audited, lets an attacker quietly attach a device to steal data or introduce malicious code.

rules.title: The session initiation information is collected
rules.explanation: Auditing /var/run/utmp, /var/log/wtmp, and /var/log/btmp records every login and logout session. This is basic information for incident investigation and for detecting unauthorized access.
rules.impact: Without auditing session files, an attacker can alter wtmp/utmp to hide their presence. Login and logout logs are the first records examined during incident investigation.

rules.title: The login and logout events are collected
rules.explanation: Auditing /var/log/faillog and /var/log/lastlog records failed login attempts and information about the most recent logins. This detects password-guessing attacks and unauthorized logins.
rules.impact: Without auditing login events, a successful unauthorized login or systematic password guessing cannot be detected. An attacker can log in and leave no trace in the audit logs.

rules.title: The unlink file deletion events by users are collected
rules.explanation: The audit configuration watches file deletion by users. The system calls unlink and unlinkat are recorded with the delete tag.
rules.impact: Without auditing, an attacker can delete critical files or traces of their activity, and the course of events cannot be reconstructed during an investigation.

rules.title: The rename file deletion events by users are collected
rules.explanation: The audit configuration watches file renaming by users. The system calls rename, renameat, and renameat2 are recorded with the delete tag.
rules.impact: Without auditing, an attacker can quietly replace or move critical files and hide traces of their activity on the system.

rules.title: The events that modify the system's Mandatory Access Controls are collected
rules.explanation: The audit configuration watches changes to AppArmor mandatory access control. Writes, attribute changes, and deletions in /etc/apparmor/ and /etc/apparmor.d/ are recorded.
rules.impact: If an attacker can quietly change AppArmor profiles, they weaken mandatory access control and bypass the system security restrictions.

rules.title: The successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the chcon command are collected
rules.explanation: The configuration generates audit records for successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the chcon command, which changes the security context of files.
rules.impact: Without auditing the chcon command, an attacker can change the security context of protected files and remain unnoticed during incident investigation.

rules.title: The successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the setfacl command are collected
rules.explanation: The configuration generates audit records for successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the setfacl command, which manages access control lists (ACLs) on files and directories.
rules.impact: Without auditing the setfacl command, an attacker can widen file access through an ACL and quietly gain access to protected data.

rules.title: The successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the chacl command are collected
rules.explanation: The configuration generates audit records for successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the chacl command, which changes access control lists (ACLs) on files and directories.
rules.impact: Without auditing the chacl command, an attacker can quietly change access control lists and obtain rights on protected files and directories.

rules.title: The successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the usermod command are collected
rules.explanation: The configuration generates audit records for successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the usermod command, which modifies system account files according to the options given.
rules.impact: Without auditing the usermod command, an attacker can quietly change account parameters, raise the account privileges, and retain access to the system.

rules.title: The kernel module loading unloading and modification is collected
rules.explanation: Loading, unloading, and modifying kernel modules (init_module, finit_module, delete_module) are critical operations. Auditing them helps detect rootkit insertion.
rules.impact: An attacker with root privileges can load a kernel rootkit module to hide their presence. Without auditing module operations, this stays unnoticed even when the system is examined.

rules.title: The kernel "init_module" and "finit_module" loading unloading and modification is collected
rules.explanation: The audit configuration watches loading of kernel modules. The system calls init_module and finit_module are recorded with the modules tag.
rules.impact: Without auditing, an attacker can load a malicious kernel module, bypass protection mechanisms, and execute code with kernel privileges.

rules.title: The kernel "delete_module" loading unloading and modification is collected
rules.explanation: The audit configuration watches unloading of kernel modules. The delete_module system call is recorded with the modules tag.
rules.impact: Without auditing, an attacker can unload a protection module or replace kernel functionality and remain unnoticed while doing so.

rules.title: The audit configuration is loaded regardless of errors
rules.explanation: The configuration sets the -c flag, under which auditctl continues loading rules even when an error occurs. The return code is still a failure if at least one rule did not load.
rules.impact: Without this flag, auditctl stops loading rules at the first error, and auditd can run with no rules in effect, leaving events unrecorded.

rules.title: The audit configuration is immutable
rules.explanation: The -e 2 flag in the auditd configuration makes the audit rules immutable until the system is rebooted. This prevents an attacker with root privileges from disabling auditing.
rules.impact: Without an immutable configuration, an attacker with root rights can immediately disable auditd or delete the audit rules before performing malicious actions, completely bypassing the controls.

rules.title: The running and on disk configuration is the same
rules.explanation: The setting requires the running audit configuration to match the configuration stored on disk. Differences can occur because of how rules are loaded through augenrules and auditctl.
rules.impact: A configuration mismatch creates a false impression that requirements are met and can result in some security events not being recorded.

rules.title: The audit log files mode is configured
rules.explanation: auditd log files must have permissions no more open than 0600 (root only). This prevents unprivileged users from reading critical security events.
rules.impact: Readable audit logs expose system-event details, the security configuration, and user behavior patterns to unprivileged users, and that information is used to plan attacks.

rules.title: The audit log files owner is configured
rules.explanation: auditd log files must be owned by the root user. This ensures that only the superuser has full control over the audit logs.
rules.impact: Audit files owned by an unprivileged user can be modified or deleted by that user to conceal information. This breaks the integrity of the logs as evidence.

rules.title: The audit log files group owner is configured
rules.explanation: auditd log files must belong to the root group. This limits log access to members of the root group and prevents unauthorized reading.
rules.impact: Audit logs in a group with broad access can be read by members of that group. This reveals details of privileged actions and can be used to plan privilege escalation.

rules.title: The audit log file directory mode is configured
rules.explanation: The /var/log/audit directory must have mode 0700 or 0750 so that only root can access its contents. Open access to the directory negates the protection of individual files.
rules.impact: Even when files are protected with mode 0600, a directory with mode 755 lets any user list its contents and use file metadata (size, date) to infer system activity.

rules.title: The audit configuration files mode is configured
rules.explanation: auditd configuration files (/etc/audit/*.conf, *.rules) must have permissions no more open than 0640. This prevents unauthorized reading and modification of audit rules.
rules.impact: Writable auditd configuration files let an attacker change the audit rules and remove monitoring of their own actions. This is a classic way to evade detection after a compromise.

rules.title: The audit configuration files owner is configured
rules.explanation: auditd configuration files must be owned by root. This prevents unprivileged users from modifying audit rules without authorization.
rules.impact: An auditd configuration file owned by an unprivileged user can be changed by that user to create blind spots in the audit system. An attacker can exclude their own actions from monitoring.

rules.title: The audit configuration files group owner is configured
rules.explanation: auditd configuration files must belong to the root group. This ensures that only privileged users can change the audit policy.
rules.impact: Configuration files in a group with broad membership let any member of the group change the audit rules. A privileged insider can then disable auditing of their own actions.

rules.title: The audit tools mode is configured
rules.explanation: auditd utilities (auditctl, aureport, ausearch, and others) must have permissions no more open than 0755, with the execute bit only for root. This prevents unauthorized manipulation of the audit system.
rules.impact: Writable auditd utilities can be replaced with malicious versions. An attacker can replace auditctl with a script that ignores audit-control commands or returns forged data.

rules.title: The audit tools owner is configured
rules.explanation: All auditd utilities must be owned by root. This ensures that only the superuser can change or replace the utilities, which the audit system can readily track.
rules.impact: An audit utility owned by an unprivileged user can be replaced by that user with a malicious version. A compromised auditctl can accept commands without actually applying them.

rules.title: The audit tools group owner is configured
rules.explanation: auditd utilities must belong to the root group. This is part of protecting the audit infrastructure against unauthorized modification and replacement.
rules.impact: Audit tools in a group with broad access can be modified by members of the group. Replacing audit utilities lets an attacker hide their presence from administrators who use those tools.

rules.title: AIDE is installed
rules.explanation: AIDE (Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment) is a file-integrity system. It creates a database of file hashes and detects unauthorized changes in the filesystem.
rules.impact: Without AIDE, an attacker can change system files, binaries, or configurations and remain unnoticed. Integrity checking is the only way to detect such changes after the fact.

rules.title: The filesystem integrity is regularly checked
rules.explanation: AIDE must run regularly (through cron or a systemd timer) to check filesystem integrity. Only periodic checks have practical value.
rules.impact: AIDE without regular checks is of no use: changes are found only on a manual run. An attacker can change files and stay unnoticed for months until the next manual check.

rules.title: The cryptographic mechanisms are used to protect the integrity of audit tools
rules.explanation: The setting requires the integrity of audit utilities to be protected by cryptographic mechanisms, for example checksums in aide.conf. Any change to the utilities must be detected.
rules.impact: An attacker can replace audit utilities or insert code into them in order to hide and delete information about their activity from the logs.

rules.title: The access to /etc/passwd is configured
rules.explanation: The file /etc/passwd contains user account information and is used by many system utilities. The setting defines permissions so utilities can read the file, while write access is limited to the root user.
rules.impact: If permissions on /etc/passwd are too weak, an attacker can change account information, raise their privileges, or create a hidden user.

rules.title: The access to /etc/passwd- is configured
rules.explanation: The file /etc/passwd- stores a backup of user account information. The setting defines permissions on this file so that write access is limited to the root user.
rules.impact: If permissions on /etc/passwd- are too weak, an attacker can replace the account backup and restore previously changed or deleted entries.

rules.title: The access to /etc/group is configured
rules.explanation: The file /etc/group contains the list of all groups defined on the system. The setting defines permissions: read and write for root, and read for other users.
rules.impact: If unprivileged users can modify /etc/group, they can add themselves to privileged groups and gain access to protected resources.

rules.title: The access to /etc/group- is configured
rules.explanation: The file /etc/group- stores a backup of the list of all groups defined on the system. The setting defines permissions on this file so that write access is limited to the root user.
rules.impact: If permissions on /etc/group- are too weak, an attacker can replace the group-list backup and restore unwanted membership in privileged groups.

rules.title: The access to /etc/shadow is configured
rules.explanation: The file /etc/shadow stores security-critical account information, including password hashes and parameters that govern how long they remain valid. The setting limits read and write access to the root user.
rules.impact: If the file is readable, an attacker can run a password-cracking program against the hashes and obtain user passwords, along with account expiration data.

rules.title: The access to /etc/shadow- is configured
rules.explanation: The file /etc/shadow- stores a backup of security-critical account information, including password hashes. The setting limits read and write access to the root user.
rules.impact: If permissions on /etc/shadow- are too weak, an attacker can read password hashes from the backup, crack them, and gain access to the accounts.

rules.title: The access to /etc/gshadow is configured
rules.explanation: The file /etc/gshadow stores security-critical group information, including group password hashes and the list of administrators. The setting limits read and write access to the root user.
rules.impact: If the file is readable, an attacker can crack group passwords from the hashes, and the group-administrator information helps them take control of those groups.

rules.title: The access to /etc/gshadow- is configured
rules.explanation: The file /etc/gshadow- stores a backup of security-critical group information, including password hashes. The setting limits read and write access to the root user.
rules.impact: If permissions on /etc/gshadow- are too weak, an attacker can read group password hashes from the backup and obtain the privileges of those groups.

rules.title: The access to /etc/shells is configured
rules.explanation: The file /etc/shells contains the full paths of valid command shells and is used by the chsh command and other programs. The setting defines permissions on this file so that write access is limited to the root user.
rules.impact: If outsiders can write the file, an attacker can add a malicious shell, and it will be treated as valid when a user shell is changed.

rules.title: The access to /etc/security/opasswd is configured
rules.explanation: The files /etc/security/opasswd and its backup /etc/security/opasswd.old contain previous user passwords when pam_unix or pam_pwhistory is in use. The setting limits read and write access to the root user.
rules.impact: If the files are readable, an attacker uses previous passwords to guess current ones and regain access to user accounts.

rules.title: The world writable files and directories are secured
rules.explanation: Files and directories with the world-writable bit (o+w) are writable by any user on the system. Such objects must either have the sticky bit set or be corrected.
rules.impact: World-writable files without the sticky bit let any user overwrite their contents. Malicious replacement of system scripts or configurations leads to system compromise or a denial of service.
rules.scope: Local filesystems scanned for world-writable files and directories

rules.title: No files or directories without an owner and a group exist
rules.explanation: Files with no owner (orphaned files) may belong to a deleted account whose UID will be reused. This gives a new user unintended access to someone else's data.
rules.impact: A file with no owner belongs to a UID that does not exist. If that UID is reassigned to a new user, that user automatically receives rights on all orphaned files, including potentially confidential data.
rules.scope: Local filesystems scanned for unowned files

rules.title: SUID and SGID files are reviewed
rules.explanation: A file owner can allow the file to run with the owner or group rights even when the user who starts it does not have those rights. The setting requires regular review of files with the SUID and SGID bits set.
rules.impact: An unknown program with the SUID or SGID bit lets an attacker run code with elevated privileges and fully compromise the system.
rules.scope: Local filesystems scanned for SUID and SGID files

rules.title: The accounts in /etc/passwd use shadowed passwords
rules.explanation: Every account in /etc/passwd must use shadowed passwords (password field = 'x'). Passwords must not be stored directly in /etc/passwd, which is readable by everyone.
rules.impact: A password stored directly in /etc/passwd, which any user can read, immediately exposes the hash for an offline attack. Shadow passwords move the hashes into /etc/shadow, where access is restricted.

rules.title: /etc/shadow password fields are not empty
rules.explanation: An empty password field in /etc/shadow means the account has no password. Such accounts must be locked or assigned a password.
rules.impact: An account with an empty password field in /etc/shadow can be reached without authentication through some PAM services that use the nullok option. This is immediate unauthorized access with no barrier.

rules.title: All groups in /etc/passwd exist in /etc/group
rules.explanation: Over time, administrative errors and system changes leave groups defined in /etc/passwd missing from /etc/group. The setting checks that every group from /etc/passwd exists in /etc/group.
rules.impact: A group that is missing from /etc/group is not managed properly, so its rights can be used for unauthorized access to files and resources.

rules.title: The shadow group is empty
rules.explanation: The shadow group gives system programs read access to /etc/shadow. The setting requires that no user be a member of this group.
rules.impact: A user in the shadow group can read password hashes from /etc/shadow and crack them, and can also use expiration data to take over accounts.

rules.title: No duplicate UIDs exist
rules.explanation: Each user must have a unique UID. Duplicate UIDs mean several accounts share one identifier, which breaks access separation.
rules.impact: Two users with the same UID have identical rights to each other's files. An attacker can create an account with the target user's UID and gain access to all of that user's files.

rules.title: No duplicate GIDs exist
rules.explanation: Each group must have a unique GID. Duplicate GIDs create ambiguity in access checks and can cause unpredictable system behavior.
rules.impact: Duplicate GIDs can give two different groups the same rights on files. This can be used to expand access by creating a group with the GID of a privileged group.

rules.title: No duplicate user names exist
rules.explanation: User names must be unique in /etc/passwd. Duplicate names with different UIDs create confusion in authentication and auditing.
rules.impact: Two accounts with the same name but different UIDs create ambiguity: tools may use one account while authentication systems use the other. This is a way to bypass access policies.

rules.title: No duplicate group names exist
rules.explanation: Group names must be unique in /etc/group. Duplicate names with different GIDs create ambiguity when managing access rights.
rules.impact: Two groups with the same name can be handled differently by different system tools. An attacker can exploit that ambiguity to obtain the privileges of the intended group.

rules.title: The local interactive user home directories are configured
rules.explanation: All interactive users must have home directories that exist. A missing home directory can cause unpredictable application behavior and store files in unintended places.
rules.impact: A user without a home directory may create files in the current working directory (/, /tmp). This can create files in system directories or cause conflicts with other users.

rules.title: The local interactive user dot files access is configured
rules.explanation: Dot files in home directories (.bashrc, .profile, .ssh/config) must not be writable by other users. Changing these files allows code that runs at login to be inserted.
rules.impact: A dot file writable by another user allows malicious code to be inserted into it. On the target user's next login, that code runs with their privileges, which is a classic path for lateral movement.

rules.title: The local interactive user dot directories access is configured
rules.explanation: Hidden directories in a user's home directory, such as .ssh, .gnupg, .config, and .cache, store personal settings, state, and key material. The setting defines safe permissions on these directories, which a user can easily change.
rules.impact: Excessive permissions allow reading and changing other users' data: for example, write access to .ssh makes it possible to add a key to authorized_keys and impersonate the owner.
